Paired with <a href="/wiki/Prem_Nazir" title="Prem Nazir">Prem Nazir</a>, they hold the <a href="/wiki/Guinness_World_Record" class="mw-redirect" title="Guinness World Record">Guinness World Record</a> for acting in the largest number of films (around 105) together as heroine and hero. She had also appeared in another 20 films with Prem Nazir, even as his mother in a film.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Sheela is a four-time winner of <a href="/wiki/Kerala_State_Film_Award" class="mw-redirect" title="Kerala State Film Award">Kerala State Film Award</a>. She came back to acting in 2003 through <i><a href="/wiki/Manassinakkare" title="Manassinakkare">Manassinakkare</a></i> after 22 years. In 2005, she won the <a href="/wiki/National_Film_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress" class="mw-redirect" title="National Film Award for Best Supporting Actress">National Film Award for Best Supporting Actress</a> for her role in the Malayalam film <i><a href="/wiki/Akale" title="Akale">Akale</a></i>. In 2019, Sheela was honoured with the <a href="/wiki/J._C._Daniel_Award" title="J. C. Daniel Award">J C Daniel Award</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Government_of_Kerala" title="Government of Kerala">Kerala government's</a> highest honour for outstanding contribution to Malayalam cinema. She was also one of the highest paid actresses, reportedly paid more than her male counterparts, of her time.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

</p><p></p></div><div name="University of Kerala" term="University of Kerala" wikidataID="Q1552247" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kerala" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: University of Kerala<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kerala">University of Kerala</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>University of Kerala</b>, commonly referred to as <b>Kerala University</b> (<b>KU</b>, <a href="/wiki/ISO_15919" title="ISO 15919">ISO</a>: <span title="International Alphabet of Sanskrit transliteration"><i lang="sa-Latn">K&#275;ra&#7735;a Sarvak&#257;l&#257;&#347;&#257;la</i></span>), formerly known as <b>University of Travancore</b> is a <a href="/wiki/Public_university" title="Public university">public</a> <a href="/wiki/State_university_(India)" title="State university (India)">state university</a> in <a href="/wiki/Thiruvananthapuram" title="Thiruvananthapuram">thiruvananthapuram</a>, the capital of <a href="/wiki/Kerala" title="Kerala">Kerala</a>, India. It was established in 1937 by a promulgation of the <a href="/wiki/Maharajah_of_Travancore" class="mw-redirect" title="Maharajah of Travancore">Maharajah of Travancore</a>, <a href="/wiki/Chithira_Thirunal_Balarama_Varma" title="Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma">Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma</a> who was also the first Chancellor of the university. <a href="/wiki/C._P._Ramaswamy_Iyer" class="mw-redirect" title="C. P. Ramaswamy Iyer">C. P. Ramaswamy Iyer</a>, the then Diwan (Prime Minister) of the State was the first Vice-Chancellor. It was the first university in Kerala, and among the first in the country. It is accredited by <a href="/wiki/National_Assessment_and_Accreditation_Council" title="National Assessment and Accreditation Council">NAAC</a> with highest grade of 'A++' and scored 3.67 points out of 4.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Anoplocnemis_curvipes.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Anoplocnemis_curvipes.jpg/250px-Anoplocnemis_curvipes.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="349" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Anoplocnemis_curvipes.jpg/500px-Anoplocnemis_curvipes.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1327" data-file-height="1853"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="spices" term="spices" wikidataID="Q42527" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spices" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: spices<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spices">Spices</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">In the <a href="/wiki/Culinary_art" class="mw-redirect" title="Culinary art">culinary arts</a>, a <b>spice</b> is a <a href="/wiki/Seed" title="Seed">seed</a>, <a href="/wiki/Fruit" title="Fruit">fruit</a>, <a href="/wiki/Root" title="Root">root</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bark_(botany)" title="Bark (botany)">bark</a>, or other <a href="/wiki/Plant" title="Plant">plant</a> substance primarily used for <a href="/wiki/Flavoring" title="Flavoring">flavoring</a> or <a href="/wiki/Color" title="Color">coloring</a> food. Spices are distinguished from <a href="/wiki/Herb" title="Herb">herbs</a>, which are the leaves, flowers, or stems of plants used for <a href="/wiki/Flavoring" title="Flavoring">flavoring</a> or as a <a href="/wiki/Garnish_(food)" class="mw-redirect" title="Garnish (food)">garnish</a>. Spices and herbs are both <a href="/wiki/Seasoning" title="Seasoning">seasonings</a>. 
Spices are sometimes used in <a href="/wiki/Medicine" title="Medicine">medicine</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sacred_rite" class="mw-redirect" title="Sacred rite">religious rituals</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cosmetics" title="Cosmetics">cosmetics</a>, or <a href="/wiki/Perfume" title="Perfume">perfume</a> production. They are usually classified into spices, spice seeds, and herbal categories.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> For example, <a href="/wiki/Vanilla" title="Vanilla">vanilla</a> is commonly used as an ingredient in <a href="/wiki/Aroma_compound" class="mw-redirect" title="Aroma compound">fragrance</a> manufacturing.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Plant-based <a href="/wiki/Sweetener" title="Sweetener">sweeteners</a> such as <a href="/wiki/Sugar" title="Sugar">sugar</a> are not considered spices. 
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Spices1.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Spices1.jpg/250px-Spices1.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="184" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Spices1.jpg/500px-Spices1.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1547" data-file-height="1137"></a><figcaption>Spices at a central market in <a href="/wiki/Agadir" title="Agadir">Agadir</a>, <a href="/wiki/Morocco" title="Morocco">Morocco</a></figcaption></figure>

(&#26085;&#26412;&#40633;&#40692;)</span>, <a href="/wiki/Hepburn_romanization" title="Hepburn romanization">Hepburn</a>: <span title="Hepburn transliteration"><i lang="ja-Latn">nihon k&#333;ji kabi</i></span><span style="margin-left:.09em">)</span></span>,<sup id="cite_ref-marukome_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-marukome-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-koto_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-koto-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> is a <a href="/wiki/Mold_(fungus)" class="mw-redirect" title="Mold (fungus)">mold</a> used in <a href="/wiki/East_Asia" title="East Asia">East Asia</a> to <a href="/wiki/Saccharification" title="Saccharification">saccharify</a> rice, <a href="/wiki/Sweet_potato" title="Sweet potato">sweet potato</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Barley" title="Barley">barley</a> in the making of alcoholic beverages such as <i><a href="/wiki/Sake" title="Sake">sake</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Sh%C5%8Dch%C5%AB" title="Sh&#333;ch&#363;">sh&#333;ch&#363;</a></i>, and also to <a href="/wiki/Fermentation_(food)" class="mw-redirect" title="Fermentation (food)">ferment</a> <a href="/wiki/Soybean" title="Soybean">soybeans</a> for making <a href="/wiki/Soy_sauce" title="Soy sauce">soy sauce</a> and <i><a href="/wiki/Miso" title="Miso">miso</a></i>. It is one of the different <a href="/wiki/Koji_(food)" class="mw-redirect" title="Koji (food)">koji molds</a> used for food fermentation.

You can <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_wizard" title="Wikipedia:Article wizard">create a draft and submit it for review</a> or <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_creation/Redirects" title="Wikipedia:Articles for creation/Redirects">request that a redirect be created</a>, but consider checking the search results below to see whether the topic is already covered.</i></p><p></p></div><div name="weedy rice" term="weedy rice" wikidataID="Q7979371" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weedy_rice" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: weedy rice<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weedy_rice">Weedy rice</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Weedy rice</b>, also known as <b>red rice</b>, is a variety of <a href="/wiki/Rice" title="Rice">rice</a> (<i><a href="/wiki/Oryza" title="Oryza">Oryza</a></i>) that produces far fewer grains per plant than cultivated rice and is therefore considered a pest. The name "weedy rice" is used for all types and variations of rice which show some characteristic features of cultivated rice and grow as weeds in commercial rice fields. Populations of weedy rice are found in many rice-growing regions.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Weedy rice varieties generally have fragile stalks that self-seed before harvest. Variations of weedy rice adapt to a wide range of natural conditions.<sup id="cite_ref-news_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-news-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ucbiotech_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ucbiotech-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ejbiotech_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ejbiotech-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p></p></div><div name="Azolla" term="Azolla" wikidataID="Q1128633" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azolla" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Azolla<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azolla">Azolla</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><i><b>Azolla</b></i> (commonly called <b>mosquito fern</b>, <b>water fern</b>, and <b>fairy moss</b>) is a <a href="/wiki/Genus" title="Genus">genus</a> of seven species of <a href="/wiki/Aquatic_plant" title="Aquatic plant">aquatic</a> <a href="/wiki/Fern" title="Fern">ferns</a> in the family <a href="/wiki/Salviniaceae" title="Salviniaceae">Salviniaceae</a>. They are extremely reduced in form and specialized, having a significantly different appearance to other ferns and more resembling some <a href="/wiki/Moss" title="Moss">mosses</a> or even <a href="/wiki/Lemnoideae" title="Lemnoideae">duckweeds</a>. <i><a href="/wiki/Azolla_filiculoides" title="Azolla filiculoides">Azolla filiculoides</a></i> is one of two fern species for which a reference genome has been published.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It is believed that this genus grew so prolifically during the <a href="/wiki/Eocene" title="Eocene">Eocene</a> (and thus absorbed such a large amount of carbon) that it triggered a global cooling event that has lasted to the present.<sup id="cite_ref-Speelman-2009_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Speelman-2009-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Azolla_caroliniana0.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Azolla_caroliniana0.jpg/250px-Azolla_caroliniana0.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Azolla_caroliniana0.jpg/500px-Azolla_caroliniana0.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="480"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="check varieties" term="check varieties" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=check%20varieties" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: check varieties<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=check%20varieties">check varieties</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">

While the exact definition of a bacterial <a href="/wiki/Phylum" title="Phylum">phylum</a> is debated, a popular definition is that a bacterial phylum is a <a href="/wiki/Monophyly" title="Monophyly">monophyletic</a> lineage of bacteria whose <a href="/wiki/16S_ribosomal_RNA" title="16S ribosomal RNA">16S rRNA genes</a> share a pairwise sequence identity of ~75% or less with those of the members of other bacterial phyla.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:A_Novel_Representation_Of_The_Tree_Of_Life.png" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/A_Novel_Representation_Of_The_Tree_Of_Life.png/500px-A_Novel_Representation_Of_The_Tree_Of_Life.png" decoding="async" width="500" height="588" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/A_Novel_Representation_Of_The_Tree_Of_Life.png/960px-A_Novel_Representation_Of_The_Tree_Of_Life.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/98/A_Novel_Representation_Of_The_Tree_Of_Life.png 2x" data-file-width="1230" data-file-height="1446"></a><figcaption>Phylogenetic tree showing the diversity of Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukaryota.<sup id="cite_ref-:16_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:16-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Major lineages are assigned arbitrary colours and named, with well-characterized lineage names, in italics. Lineages lacking an isolated representative are highlighted with non-italicized names and red dots.  </figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="Pearl Millet" term="Pearl Millet" wikidataID="Q50840653" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Millet" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Pearl Millet<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Millet">Pearl Millet</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Pearl millet</b> (<i><b>Cenchrus americanus</b></i>, commonly known as the synonym <i>Pennisetum  glaucum</i>) is the most widely grown type of <a href="/wiki/Millet" title="Millet">millet</a>. It has been grown in <a href="/wiki/Africa" title="Africa">Africa</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</a> since prehistoric times. The center of diversity and suggested area of <a href="/wiki/Domestication" title="Domestication">domestication</a> for the crop is in the <a href="/wiki/Sahel" title="Sahel">Sahel</a> zone of <a href="/wiki/West_Africa" title="West Africa">West Africa</a>.
</p>
<div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Grain_millet,_early_grain_fill,_Tifton,_7-3-02.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Grain_millet%2C_early_grain_fill%2C_Tifton%2C_7-3-02.jpg/250px-Grain_millet%2C_early_grain_fill%2C_Tifton%2C_7-3-02.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Grain_millet%2C_early_grain_fill%2C_Tifton%2C_7-3-02.jpg/500px-Grain_millet%2C_early_grain_fill%2C_Tifton%2C_7-3-02.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="768"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="pointed gourd" term="pointed gourd" wikidataID="Q2724295" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointed_gourd" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: pointed gourd<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointed_gourd">Pointed gourd</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><i><b>Trichosanthes dioica</b></i>, also known as <b>pointed gourd</b>, is a tropical perennial cucurbit plant with its origin in the Indian subcontinent. The plant propagated vegetatively and grows with training on a support system (e.g., trellis) as pencil-thick vines (creepers) with dark-green cordate (heart-shaped) simple leaves. It is a well-developed dioecious plants having distinct male and female flowers on staminate and pistillate plants, respectively. The fruits are green with white or no stripes' and have unpalatable seeds. Size can vary from small and round to thick and long &#8211; 5&#8211;15 centimetres (2&#8211;6 inches). It thrives well under a hot to moderately warm and humid climate. The plant remains dormant during the winter season and prefers fertile, well-drained sandy loam soil due to its susceptibility to water-logging.<sup id="cite_ref-Next_generation_sequencing_and_tran_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Next_generation_sequencing_and_tran-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-In_vitro_propagation_of_Trichosanth_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-In_vitro_propagation_of_Trichosanth-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

Worldwide they are responsible for a considerable amount of economic damage to many important crops such as <a href="/wiki/Tomato" title="Tomato">tomatoes</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bean" title="Bean">beans</a>, <a href="/wiki/Squash_(plant)" class="mw-redirect" title="Squash (plant)">squash</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cassava" title="Cassava">cassava</a> and <a href="/wiki/Cotton" title="Cotton">cotton</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ViralZone_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ViralZone-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> There are 464 species in this genus.<sup id="cite_ref-ICTV_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ICTV-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

even in English &#8211; by its Spanish acronym <b>CIMMYT</b> for <i><b>Centro Internacional de Mejoramiento de Ma&#237;z y Trigo</b></i>) is a non-profit research-for-development organization that develops improved varieties of <a href="/wiki/Wheat" title="Wheat">wheat</a> and <a href="/wiki/Maize" title="Maize">maize</a> with the aim of contributing to <a href="/wiki/Food_security" title="Food security">food security</a>, and innovates agricultural practices to help boost production, prevent crop disease and improve <a href="/wiki/Smallholding" title="Smallholding">smallholder</a> farmers' livelihoods.<sup id="cite_ref-cimmyt_1-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cimmyt-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> CIMMYT is one of the 15 <a href="/wiki/CGIAR" title="CGIAR">CGIAR centers</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-CGIAR_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CGIAR-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> CIMMYT is known for hosting the world's largest maize and wheat genebank at its headquarters in Mexico.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

Examples of <a href="/wiki/Manual_labour" title="Manual labour">human-powered</a> tilling methods using <a href="/wiki/Hand_tool" title="Hand tool">hand tools</a> include <a href="/wiki/Shovel" title="Shovel">shoveling</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pickaxe" title="Pickaxe">picking</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mattock" title="Mattock">mattock</a> work, <a href="/wiki/Hoe_(tool)" title="Hoe (tool)">hoeing</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Rake_(tool)" title="Rake (tool)">raking</a>. Examples of <a href="/wiki/Working_animal" title="Working animal">draft-animal-powered</a> or <a href="/wiki/Mechanization" title="Mechanization">mechanized</a> work include <a href="/wiki/Plough" title="Plough">ploughing</a> (overturning with moldboards or chiseling with chisel shanks), <a href="/wiki/Rotary_tiller" class="mw-redirect" title="Rotary tiller">rototilling</a>, rolling with <a href="/wiki/Cultipacker" title="Cultipacker">cultipackers</a> or other <a href="/wiki/Roller_(agricultural_tool)" title="Roller (agricultural tool)">rollers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Harrow_(tool)" title="Harrow (tool)">harrowing</a>, and cultivating with <a href="/wiki/Cultivator" title="Cultivator">cultivator</a> shanks (teeth).
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tillage.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Tillage.jpg/250px-Tillage.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="170" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Tillage.jpg/500px-Tillage.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2727"></a><figcaption>Tillage after corn harvest <br> (<a class="external text" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tillage%20video.webm">Click for video</a>)</figcaption></figure>

Halotolerant organisms on the other hand (belonging to different <a href="/wiki/Domain_(biology)" title="Domain (biology)">domains</a> of life) can grow under saline conditions, but do not require elevated concentrations of salt for growth. <a href="/wiki/Halophyte" title="Halophyte">Halophytes</a> are salt-tolerant higher plants. Halotolerant microorganisms are of considerable biotechnological interest.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<p></p></div><div name="neem cake" term="neem cake" wikidataID="Q6986851" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neem_cake" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: neem cake<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neem_cake">Neem cake</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Neem cake organic manure</b> is the by-product obtained in the process of cold pressing of <a href="/wiki/Neem" class="mw-redirect" title="Neem">neem</a> tree fruits and kernels, and the <a href="/wiki/Solvent_extraction" class="mw-redirect" title="Solvent extraction">solvent extraction</a> process for <a href="/wiki/Neem_oil" title="Neem oil">neem oil</a> cake.
It is a potential source of organic manure under the <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Indian_Standards" title="Bureau of Indian Standards">Bureau of Indian Standards</a>, Specification No. 8558. Neem has demonstrated considerable potential as a fertilizer. For this purpose, neem cake and neem leaves are especially promising. Puri (1999), in his book Neem&#160;: The Divine Tree Azadirachta,<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> has given details about neem seed cake as manure and <a href="/wiki/Nitrification" title="Nitrification">nitrification</a> inhibitor.  The author has described that, after processing, neem cake can be used for partial replacement of poultry and cattle feed.
</p>

</div><p></p></div><div name="heat stress" term="heat stress" wikidataID="Q242165" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_stress" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: heat stress<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_stress">Heat stress</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Hyperthermia</b>, also known as <b>overheating</b>, is a condition in which an individual's body temperature is elevated beyond normal due to failed <a href="/wiki/Thermoregulation" title="Thermoregulation">thermoregulation</a>. The person's body produces or absorbs more <a href="/wiki/Heat" title="Heat">heat</a> than it dissipates. According to the <i>International Emergency Medicine Education Project</i>, severe hyperthermia (body temperature elevation of beyond 40&#160;&#176;C (104&#160;&#176;F)) "becomes a <a href="/wiki/Medical_emergency" title="Medical emergency">medical emergency</a> requiring immediate treatment to prevent disability or death".<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Almost half a million deaths are recorded every year from hyperthermia.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Clinical_thermometer_38.7.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Clinical_thermometer_38.7.JPG/250px-Clinical_thermometer_38.7.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Clinical_thermometer_38.7.JPG/500px-Clinical_thermometer_38.7.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="3112" data-file-height="1927"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="biochemical traits" term="biochemical traits" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=biochemical%20traits" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: biochemical traits<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=biochemical%20traits">biochemical traits</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">

There are several species of grain called rice.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Oryza_sativa" title="Oryza sativa">Asian rice</a> (<i>Oryza sativa)</i> is most widely known and most widely grown, with two major subspecies (<i>indica</i> and <i>japonica</i>) and over 40,000 varieties.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Also included in this list are varieties of <a href="/wiki/Oryza_glaberrima" title="Oryza glaberrima">African rice</a> (<i>Oryza glaberrima</i>) and <a href="/wiki/Wild_rice" title="Wild rice">wild rice</a> (genus <i>Zizania</i>).
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Rice_grains_(IRRI).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Rice_grains_%28IRRI%29.jpg/250px-Rice_grains_%28IRRI%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Rice_grains_%28IRRI%29.jpg/500px-Rice_grains_%28IRRI%29.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3600" data-file-height="2400"></a><figcaption>Rice can come in many shapes, colours and sizes.</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="sugarcane cultivation" term="sugarcane cultivation" wikidataID="Q36940" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarcane_cultivation" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: sugarcane cultivation<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarcane_cultivation">Sugarcane cultivation</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Sugarcane</b> or <b>sugar cane</b> is a species of tall, <a href="/wiki/Perennial_plant" class="mw-redirect" title="Perennial plant">perennial</a> grass (in the genus <i><a href="/wiki/Saccharum" title="Saccharum">Saccharum</a></i>, tribe <a href="/wiki/Andropogoneae" title="Andropogoneae">Andropogoneae</a>) that is used for <a href="/wiki/Sugar" title="Sugar">sugar</a> <a href="/wiki/Sugar_industry" title="Sugar industry">production</a>. The plants are 2&#8211;6 m (6&#8211;20 ft) tall with stout, jointed, fibrous stalks that are rich in <a href="/wiki/Sucrose" title="Sucrose">sucrose</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> which accumulates in the <a href="/wiki/Plant_stem" title="Plant stem">stalk internodes</a>. Sugarcanes belong to the grass family, <a href="/wiki/Poaceae" title="Poaceae">Poaceae</a>, an economically important <a href="/wiki/Flowering_plant" title="Flowering plant">flowering plant</a> family that includes maize, wheat, rice, and <a href="/wiki/Sorghum" title="Sorghum">sorghum</a>, and many <a href="/wiki/Forage" title="Forage">forage</a> crops. It is native to <a href="/wiki/New_Guinea" title="New Guinea">New Guinea</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-POWO_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-POWO-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Saccharum_officinarum_-_K%C3%B6hler%E2%80%93s_Medizinal-Pflanzen-125.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Saccharum_officinarum_-_K%C3%B6hler%E2%80%93s_Medizinal-Pflanzen-125.jpg/250px-Saccharum_officinarum_-_K%C3%B6hler%E2%80%93s_Medizinal-Pflanzen-125.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="340" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/74/Saccharum_officinarum_-_K%C3%B6hler%E2%80%93s_Medizinal-Pflanzen-125.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="437" data-file-height="595"></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Saccharum_officinarum" title="Saccharum officinarum">Saccharum officinarum</a></i></figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="Plant Physiology" term="Plant Physiology" wikidataID="Q185973" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_Physiology" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Plant Physiology<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_Physiology">Plant Physiology</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Plant physiology</b> is a subdiscipline of <a href="/wiki/Botany" title="Botany">botany</a> concerned with the functioning, or <a href="/wiki/Physiology" title="Physiology">physiology</a>, of <a href="/wiki/Plant" title="Plant">plants</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Salisbury_&amp;_Ross_1992_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Salisbury_&amp;_Ross_1992-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kiemtafel_(germination_table).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Kiemtafel_%28germination_table%29.jpg/250px-Kiemtafel_%28germination_table%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="135" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Kiemtafel_%28germination_table%29.jpg/330px-Kiemtafel_%28germination_table%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Kiemtafel_%28germination_table%29.jpg/500px-Kiemtafel_%28germination_table%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2272" data-file-height="1704"></a><figcaption>A germination rate experiment</figcaption></figure></div><p></p></div><div name="Thailand" term="Thailand" wikidataID="Q869" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Thailand<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand">Thailand</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Thailand</b>,<sup id="cite_ref-endo_10-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-endo-10"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>iii<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> officially the <b>Kingdom of Thailand</b>,<sup id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>iv<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and formerly known as <b>Siam</b> until 1939,<sup id="cite_ref-siam_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-siam-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>v<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> is a country located in <a href="/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia" title="Mainland Southeast Asia">mainland Southeast Asia</a>. It shares land borders with <a href="/wiki/Myanmar" title="Myanmar">Myanmar</a> to the west and northwest, <a href="/wiki/Laos" title="Laos">Laos</a> to the east and northeast, <a href="/wiki/Cambodia" title="Cambodia">Cambodia</a> to the southeast, and <a href="/wiki/Malaysia" title="Malaysia">Malaysia</a> to the south. Its maritime boundaries include the <a href="/wiki/Gulf_of_Thailand" title="Gulf of Thailand">Gulf of Thailand</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Andaman_Sea" title="Andaman Sea">Andaman Sea</a>, as well as maritime borders with <a href="/wiki/Vietnam" title="Vietnam">Vietnam</a>, <a href="/wiki/Indonesia" title="Indonesia">Indonesia</a>, and <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a>. Thailand has a population of nearly 66 million people<sup id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and covers an area of approximately 513,115&#160;km<sup>2</sup> (198,115 sq mi).<sup id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The country's <a href="/wiki/Capital_city" title="Capital city">capital</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Thailand#Largest_cities_by_urban_population" title="List of municipalities in Thailand">largest city</a> is <a href="/wiki/Bangkok" title="Bangkok">Bangkok</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kingdom_%26_People_of_Siam_(Vol_1,_1857,_15).svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Kingdom_%26_People_of_Siam_%28Vol_1%2C_1857%2C_15%29.svg/250px-Kingdom_%26_People_of_Siam_%28Vol_1%2C_1857%2C_15%29.svg.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="63" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Kingdom_%26_People_of_Siam_%28Vol_1%2C_1857%2C_15%29.svg/500px-Kingdom_%26_People_of_Siam_%28Vol_1%2C_1857%2C_15%29.svg.png 1.5x" data-file-width="1688" data-file-height="428"></a><figcaption><i>SPPM Mongkut Rex Siamensium</i>, <a href="/wiki/King_Mongkut" class="mw-redirect" title="King Mongkut">King Mongkut</a>'s signature</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="Agricultural Extension" term="Agricultural Extension" wikidataID="Q4693964" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Extension" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Agricultural Extension<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_Extension">Agricultural Extension</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Agricultural extension</b> is the application of scientific research and new knowledge to <a href="/wiki/Agricultural" class="mw-redirect" title="Agricultural">agricultural</a> practices through <a href="/wiki/Farmer" title="Farmer">farmer</a> <a href="/wiki/Education" title="Education">education</a>. The field of 'extension' now encompasses a wider range of communication and learning activities organized for <a href="/wiki/Rural_area" title="Rural area">rural</a> people by educators from different disciplines, including <a href="/wiki/Agriculture" title="Agriculture">agriculture</a>, <a href="/wiki/Agricultural_marketing" title="Agricultural marketing">agricultural marketing</a>, <a href="/wiki/Health" title="Health">health</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Business_studies" title="Business studies">business studies</a>.

The fiber is almost pure <a href="/wiki/Cellulose" title="Cellulose">cellulose</a> and may contain minor percentages of waxes, fats, pectins, and water. Under natural conditions, cotton bolls facilitate the dispersal of the seeds.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:BALLS_OF_COTTON_(ANDHRA_-SOUTH_INDIA)_READY_FOR_HARVEST.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/BALLS_OF_COTTON_%28ANDHRA_-SOUTH_INDIA%29_READY_FOR_HARVEST.jpg/250px-BALLS_OF_COTTON_%28ANDHRA_-SOUTH_INDIA%29_READY_FOR_HARVEST.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/BALLS_OF_COTTON_%28ANDHRA_-SOUTH_INDIA%29_READY_FOR_HARVEST.jpg/500px-BALLS_OF_COTTON_%28ANDHRA_-SOUTH_INDIA%29_READY_FOR_HARVEST.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="5400" data-file-height="3600"></a><figcaption>Cotton ready for harvest in <a href="/wiki/Andhra_Pradesh" title="Andhra Pradesh">Andhra Pradesh</a>, India.</figcaption></figure>

</p>
<div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Paspalum_scrobiculatum_224164066.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Paspalum_scrobiculatum_224164066.jpg/250px-Paspalum_scrobiculatum_224164066.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Paspalum_scrobiculatum_224164066.jpg/500px-Paspalum_scrobiculatum_224164066.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1366"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="Imidacloprid" term="Imidacloprid" wikidataID="Q420098" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imidacloprid" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Imidacloprid<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imidacloprid">Imidacloprid</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Imidacloprid</b> is a systemic <a href="/wiki/Insecticide" title="Insecticide">insecticide</a> belonging to a class of chemicals called the <a href="/wiki/Neonicotinoid" title="Neonicotinoid">neonicotinoids</a> which act on the <a href="/wiki/Central_nervous_system" title="Central nervous system">central nervous system</a> of insects. The chemical works by interfering with the transmission of stimuli in the insect nervous system. Specifically, it causes a blockage of the <a href="/wiki/Nicotinic" class="mw-redirect" title="Nicotinic">nicotinergic</a> neuronal pathway. By blocking <a href="/wiki/Nicotinic_acetylcholine_receptor" title="Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor">nicotinic acetylcholine receptors</a>, imidacloprid prevents <a href="/wiki/Acetylcholine" title="Acetylcholine">acetylcholine</a> from <a href="/wiki/Neurotransmitter" title="Neurotransmitter">transmitting</a> impulses between nerves, resulting in the insect's paralysis and eventual death. It is effective on contact and via stomach action.<sup id="cite_ref-extoxnet_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-extoxnet-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Because imidacloprid binds much more strongly to insect neuron <a href="/wiki/Receptor_(biochemistry)" title="Receptor (biochemistry)">receptors</a> than to mammal neuron receptors, this <a href="/wiki/Insecticide" title="Insecticide">insecticide</a> is more toxic to insects than to mammals.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGervaisLuukinenBuhlStone2010_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGervaisLuukinenBuhlStone2010-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><a href="https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q420098#P2566" title="Edit this at Wikidata"><img alt="Edit this at Wikidata" class="ext-phonos"><span data-nosnippet="" id="ooui-php-1" class="noexcerpt ext-phonos-PhonosButton oo-ui-widget oo-ui-widget-enabled oo-ui-buttonElement oo-ui-buttonElement-frameless class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <b>DNA</b>) is a <a href="/wiki/Polymer" title="Polymer">polymer</a> composed of two <a href="/wiki/Polynucleotide" title="Polynucleotide">polynucleotide</a> chains that coil around each other to form a <a href="/wiki/Nucleic_acid_double_helix" title="Nucleic acid double helix">double helix</a>. The polymer carries <a href="/wiki/Genetics" title="Genetics">genetic</a> instructions for the development, functioning, growth and <a href="/wiki/Reproduction" title="Reproduction">reproduction</a> of all known <a href="/wiki/Organism" title="Organism">organisms</a> and many <a href="/wiki/Virus" title="Virus">viruses</a>. DNA and <a href="/wiki/Ribonucleic_acid" class="mw-redirect" title="Ribonucleic acid">ribonucleic acid</a> (RNA) are <a href="/wiki/Nucleic_acid" title="Nucleic acid">nucleic acids</a>. Alongside <a href="/wiki/Protein" title="Protein">proteins</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lipids" class="mw-redirect" title="Lipids">lipids</a> and complex carbohydrates (<a href="/wiki/Polysaccharide" title="Polysaccharide">polysaccharides</a>), nucleic acids are one of the four major types of <a href="/wiki/Macromolecule" title="Macromolecule">macromolecules</a> that are essential for all known forms of <a href="/wiki/Life" title="Life">life</a>.

The weather in the tropics is dominated by the <a href="/wiki/Tropical_rain_belt" title="Tropical rain belt">tropical rain belt</a>, which moves from the northern to the southern tropics and back over the course of the year. The <a href="/wiki/Temperate" class="mw-redirect" title="Temperate">temperate</a> counterpart to the tropical dry season is <a href="/wiki/Summer" title="Summer">summer</a> or <a href="/wiki/Winter" title="Winter">winter</a>.
</p>

It is a <a href="/wiki/Glossary_of_botanical_terms#scandent" title="Glossary of botanical terms">scrambling and trailing</a> <a href="/wiki/Vine" title="Vine">vine</a>-like plant, and is <a href="/wiki/Plant_breeding" title="Plant breeding">widely cultivated</a> worldwide, with more than 1,000 <a href="/wiki/Variety_(botany)" title="Variety (botany)">varieties</a>.

</div><p></p></div><div name="maintenance" term="maintenance" wikidataID="Q1043452" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maintenance" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: maintenance<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maintenance">Maintenance</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">The technical meaning of <b>maintenance</b> involves functional checks, servicing, repairing or replacing of necessary devices, equipment, <a href="/wiki/Machinery" class="mw-redirect" title="Machinery">machinery</a>, building <a href="/wiki/Infrastructure" title="Infrastructure">infrastructure</a> and supporting utilities in industrial, business, and residential installations.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Terms such as "predictive" or "planned" maintenance describe various cost-effective practices aimed at keeping equipment operational; these activities occur either before<sup id="cite_ref-DPenn.PdM_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-DPenn.PdM-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> or after a potential failure.
</p>

Oil allows higher cooking temperatures than water, making <a href="/wiki/Cooking" title="Cooking">cooking</a> faster and more flavorful, while likewise distributing heat, reducing burning and uneven cooking. It sometimes imparts its own flavor. Cooking oil is also used in food preparation and flavoring not involving heat, such as <a href="/wiki/Salad_dressings" class="mw-redirect" title="Salad dressings">salad dressings</a> and bread dips.

An offspring is heterotic if its <a href="/wiki/Trait_(biology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Trait (biology)">traits</a> are enhanced as a result of mixing the genetic contributions of its parents. The heterotic offspring often has traits that are more than the simple addition of the parents' traits, and can be explained by <a href="/wiki/Mendelian_inheritance" title="Mendelian inheritance">Mendelian</a> or <a href="/wiki/Non-Mendelian_inheritance" title="Non-Mendelian inheritance">non-Mendelian inheritance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Typical heterotic/hybrid traits of interest in agriculture are higher yield, quicker maturity, stability, drought tolerance<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> etc.
</p>

Examples of nanocellulosic materials are <b>microfibrilated cellulose</b>, <b>cellulose <a href="/wiki/Nanofiber" title="Nanofiber">nanofibers</a></b> or <b>cellulose <a href="/wiki/Nanocrystal" class="mw-redirect" title="Nanocrystal">nanocrystals</a></b>. Nanocellulose may be obtained from natural cellulose fibers through a variety of production processes. This family of materials possesses interesting properties suitable for a wide range of potential applications.
</p>

It preserves their <a href="/wiki/Genetic_information" class="mw-redirect" title="Genetic information">genetic information</a> in the form of reproductive material like seeds, sperm, eggs, <a href="/wiki/Embryo" title="Embryo">embryos</a>, cells and other kinds of DNA. Oftentimes, these banks house the genetic material of species that are <a href="/wiki/Endangered" class="mw-redirect" title="Endangered">endangered</a> or <a href="/wiki/Extinction" title="Extinction">close to extinction.</a>They are also used for the preservation of major crop species and cultivars, in order to preserve <a href="/wiki/Crop_diversity" title="Crop diversity">crop diversity</a>.This protects the organism from threats like <a href="/wiki/Extinction" title="Extinction">extinction</a>, <a href="/wiki/Disease" title="Disease">diseases</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Climate_change" title="Climate change">climate change</a>.
</p>

pre-crisis status quickly.<sup id="cite_ref-deTerte2014_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-deTerte2014-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-APA2020_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-APA2020-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Resilience is generally understood either as a developmental process that can be cultivated over time, or as a relatively stable personality trait.<sup id="cite_ref-Masten2001_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Masten2001-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Researchers have identified numerous internal factors that influence resilience, including self-esteem, self-regulation, optimism, and emotional intelligence, as well as external factors such as social support from family, friends, and community.<sup id="cite_ref-Southwick2014_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Southwick2014-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

It is the <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population" title="List of countries and dependencies by population">eighth-most populous country</a> in the world and among the <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density" title="List of countries and dependencies by population density">most densely populated</a> with a population of over 171 million within an area of 148,460 square kilometres (57,320&#160;sq&#160;mi). Bangladesh shares land borders with <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a> to the north, west, and east, and <a href="/wiki/Myanmar" title="Myanmar">Myanmar</a> to the southeast. It has a coastline along the <a href="/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal" title="Bay of Bengal">Bay of Bengal</a> to its south and is separated from <a href="/wiki/Bhutan" title="Bhutan">Bhutan</a> and <a href="/wiki/Nepal" title="Nepal">Nepal</a> by the <a href="/wiki/Siliguri_Corridor" title="Siliguri Corridor">Siliguri Corridor</a>, and from <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a> by the <a href="/wiki/List_of_Indian_states" class="mw-redirect" title="List of Indian states">Indian state</a> of <a href="/wiki/Sikkim" title="Sikkim">Sikkim</a> to its north. <a href="/wiki/Dhaka" title="Dhaka">Dhaka</a>, the capital and <a href="/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bangladesh" title="List of cities and towns in Bangladesh">largest city</a>, is the nation's political, financial, and cultural centre. <a href="/wiki/Chittagong" title="Chittagong">Chittagong</a> is the second-largest city and <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Chittagong" title="Port of Chittagong">the busiest port</a> of the country.

Drought often has large impacts on the <a href="/wiki/Ecosystem" title="Ecosystem">ecosystems</a> and <a href="/wiki/Agriculture" title="Agriculture">agriculture</a> of affected regions, and causes harm to the local <a href="/wiki/Economy" title="Economy">economy</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Annual dry seasons in the <a href="/wiki/Tropics" title="Tropics">tropics</a> significantly increase the chances of a drought developing, with subsequent increased <a href="/wiki/Wildfire" title="Wildfire">wildfire</a> risks.<sup id="cite_ref-Brando_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brando-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Heat_wave" title="Heat wave">Heat waves</a> can significantly worsen drought conditions by increasing <a href="/wiki/Evapotranspiration" title="Evapotranspiration">evapotranspiration</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Merzdorf_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Merzdorf-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This dries out forests and other vegetation, and increases the amount of fuel for wildfires.<sup id="cite_ref-Brando_4-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brando-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Hartmann_6-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hartmann-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Fields_outside_benambra.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Fields_outside_benambra.jpg/500px-Fields_outside_benambra.jpg" decoding="async" width="400" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Fields_outside_benambra.jpg/960px-Fields_outside_benambra.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2250" data-file-height="924"></a><figcaption>Fields outside <a href="/wiki/Benambra,_Victoria" class="mw-redirect" title="Benambra, Victoria">Benambra</a>, Australia suffering from drought in 2006.</figcaption></figure>

<p></p></div><div name="Allium" term="Allium" wikidataID="Q49391" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allium" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Allium<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allium">Allium</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><i><b>Allium</b></i> is a large genus of <a href="/wiki/Monocotyledon" title="Monocotyledon">monocotyledonous</a> flowering plants with around 1000 accepted species,<sup id="cite_ref-WCSP_Allium_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WCSP_Allium-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> making <i>Allium</i> the largest genus in the family <a href="/wiki/Amaryllidaceae" title="Amaryllidaceae">Amaryllidaceae</a> and among the largest plant genera in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-frodin2004_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-frodin2004-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Many of the species are edible, and some have a long history of cultivation and human consumption as a vegetable including the <a href="/wiki/Onion" title="Onion">onion</a>, <a href="/wiki/Garlic" title="Garlic">garlic</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scallion" title="Scallion">scallions</a>, <a href="/wiki/Shallot" title="Shallot">shallots</a>, <a href="/wiki/Leek" title="Leek">leeks</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Chives" title="Chives">chives</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Ursa_ajlo_1.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Ursa_ajlo_1.jpg/250px-Ursa_ajlo_1.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="333" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Ursa_ajlo_1.jpg/500px-Ursa_ajlo_1.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2736" data-file-height="3648"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="New Delhi" term="New Delhi" wikidataID="Q987" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: New Delhi<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi">New Delhi</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>New Delhi</b><sup id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>a<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> is the <a href="/wiki/Capital_city" title="Capital city">capital city</a> of <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a> and a part of the <a href="/wiki/Delhi" title="Delhi">National Capital Territory of Delhi</a> (NCT). New Delhi is the seat of all three branches of the <a href="/wiki/Government_of_India" title="Government of India">Government of India</a>, hosting the <a href="/wiki/Rashtrapati_Bhavan,_New_Delhi" class="mw-redirect" title="Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi">Rashtrapati Bhavan</a> (Presidential Palace), <a href="/wiki/New_Parliament_House,_New_Delhi" class="mw-redirect" title="New Parliament House, New Delhi">Sansad Bhavan</a> (Parliament House), and the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_India" title="Supreme Court of India">Supreme Court</a>. New Delhi is a <a href="/wiki/Municipal_governance_in_India" title="Municipal governance in India">municipality</a> within the NCT, administered by the <a href="/wiki/New_Delhi_Municipal_Council" title="New Delhi Municipal Council">New Delhi Municipal Council</a> (NDMC), which covers mostly <a href="/wiki/Lutyens%27_Delhi" title="Lutyens' Delhi">Lutyens' Delhi</a> and a few adjacent areas. The municipal area is part of a larger <a href="/wiki/List_of_districts_in_India" title="List of districts in India">administrative district</a>, the <a href="/wiki/New_Delhi_district" title="New Delhi district">New Delhi district</a>.

You can <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_wizard" title="Wikipedia:Article wizard">create a draft and submit it for review</a> or <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_creation/Redirects" title="Wikipedia:Articles for creation/Redirects">request that a redirect be created</a>, but consider checking the search results below to see whether the topic is already covered.</i></p><p></p></div><div name="West Bengal" term="West Bengal" wikidataID="Q1356" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: West Bengal<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal">West Bengal</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>West Bengal</b><sup id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>a<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> is a <a href="/wiki/States_and_union_territories_of_India" title="States and union territories of India">state</a> in the <a href="/wiki/East_India" title="East India">eastern portion</a> of <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a>. It is situated along the <a href="/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal" title="Bay of Bengal">Bay of Bengal</a>. It had a population of over 91 million inhabitants within an area of 88,752&#160;km<sup>2</sup> (34,267&#160;sq&#160;mi) as of 2011. The population estimate as of 2023 is 99,723,000.<sup id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> West Bengal is the <a href="/wiki/List_of_states_and_union_territories_of_India_by_population" title="List of states and union territories of India by population">fourth-most populous</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_states_and_union_territories_of_India_by_area" title="List of states and union territories of India by area">thirteenth-largest state by area</a> in India, as well as the <a href="/wiki/List_of_first-level_administrative_divisions_by_population" title="List of first-level administrative divisions by population">eighth-most populous country subdivision</a> of the world. As a part of the <a href="/wiki/Bengal_region" class="mw-redirect" title="Bengal region">Bengal region</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</a>, it borders <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh" title="Bangladesh">Bangladesh</a> in the east, and <a href="/wiki/Nepal" title="Nepal">Nepal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bhutan" title="Bhutan">Bhutan</a> in the north. It also borders the Indian states of <a href="/wiki/Jharkhand" title="Jharkhand">Jharkhand</a>, <a href="/wiki/Odisha" title="Odisha">Odisha</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bihar" title="Bihar">Bihar</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sikkim" title="Sikkim">Sikkim</a> and <a href="/wiki/Assam" title="Assam">Assam</a>. The state capital is <a href="/wiki/Kolkata" title="Kolkata">Kolkata</a>, the <a href="/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_India" title="List of metropolitan areas in India">third-largest metropolis</a>, and <a href="/wiki/List_of_cities_in_India_by_population" title="List of cities in India by population">seventh largest city by population</a> in India. West Bengal includes the <a href="/wiki/Darjeeling_Himalayan_hill_region" title="Darjeeling Himalayan hill region">Darjeeling Himalayan hill region</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Ganges_delta" class="mw-redirect" title="Ganges delta">Ganges delta</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Rarh_region" title="Rarh region">Rarh region</a>, the coastal <a href="/wiki/Sundarbans" title="Sundarbans">Sundarbans</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal" title="Bay of Bengal">Bay of Bengal</a>. The state's main ethnic group are the <a href="/wiki/Bengalis" title="Bengalis">Bengalis</a>, with the <a href="/wiki/Bengali_Hindus" title="Bengali Hindus">Bengali Hindus</a> forming the demographic majority.

Insects that pose disadvantages are considered <a href="/wiki/Pest_(organism)" title="Pest (organism)">pests</a>. Some species can cause indirect damage by spreading diseases, and these are termed as disease <a href="/wiki/Vector_(epidemiology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Vector (epidemiology)">vectors</a>. Those that are beneficial include those that are reared for food such as <a href="/wiki/Honey" title="Honey">honey</a>, substances such as <a href="/wiki/Lac_(resin)" title="Lac (resin)">lac</a> or pigments, and for their role in <a href="/wiki/Pollinator" title="Pollinator">pollinating</a> crops and controlling pests.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

Examples of <a href="/wiki/Manual_labour" title="Manual labour">human-powered</a> tilling methods using <a href="/wiki/Hand_tool" title="Hand tool">hand tools</a> include <a href="/wiki/Shovel" title="Shovel">shoveling</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pickaxe" title="Pickaxe">picking</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mattock" title="Mattock">mattock</a> work, <a href="/wiki/Hoe_(tool)" title="Hoe (tool)">hoeing</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Rake_(tool)" title="Rake (tool)">raking</a>. Examples of <a href="/wiki/Working_animal" title="Working animal">draft-animal-powered</a> or <a href="/wiki/Mechanization" title="Mechanization">mechanized</a> work include <a href="/wiki/Plough" title="Plough">ploughing</a> (overturning with moldboards or chiseling with chisel shanks), <a href="/wiki/Rotary_tiller" class="mw-redirect" title="Rotary tiller">rototilling</a>, rolling with <a href="/wiki/Cultipacker" title="Cultipacker">cultipackers</a> or other <a href="/wiki/Roller_(agricultural_tool)" title="Roller (agricultural tool)">rollers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Harrow_(tool)" title="Harrow (tool)">harrowing</a>, and cultivating with <a href="/wiki/Cultivator" title="Cultivator">cultivator</a> shanks (teeth).
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tillage.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Tillage.jpg/250px-Tillage.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="170" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Tillage.jpg/500px-Tillage.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="2727"></a><figcaption>Tillage after corn harvest <br> (<a class="external text" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tillage%20video.webm">Click for video</a>)</figcaption></figure>

It is the lightweight black remnants remaining after the <a href="/wiki/Pyrolysis" title="Pyrolysis">pyrolysis</a> of <a href="/wiki/Biomass" title="Biomass">biomass</a>, consisting of <a href="/wiki/Carbon" title="Carbon">carbon</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ash_(analytical_chemistry)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ash (analytical chemistry)">ashes</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Despite its name, biochar is sterile immediately after production and only gains biological life following assisted or incidental exposure to biota. Biochar is defined by the International Biochar Initiative as the "solid material obtained from the <a href="/wiki/Thermochemical" class="mw-redirect" title="Thermochemical">thermochemical</a> conversion of biomass in an <a href="/wiki/Reducing_atmosphere" title="Reducing atmosphere">oxygen-limited</a> environment".<sup id="cite_ref-auto2_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto2-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Biochar_pile.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A large pile of biochar" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Biochar_pile.jpg/250px-Biochar_pile.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Biochar_pile.jpg/500px-Biochar_pile.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2000"></a><figcaption>A pile of biochar</figcaption></figure>

You can <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_wizard" title="Wikipedia:Article wizard">create a draft and submit it for review</a> or <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_creation/Redirects" title="Wikipedia:Articles for creation/Redirects">request that a redirect be created</a>, but consider checking the search results below to see whether the topic is already covered.</i></p><p></p></div><div name="zero tillage" term="zero tillage" wikidataID="Q1227672" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_tillage" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: zero tillage<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_tillage">Zero tillage</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>No-till farming</b> (also known as <b>zero tillage</b> or <b>direct drilling</b>) is an agricultural technique for growing crops or <a href="/wiki/Pasture" title="Pasture">pasture</a> without disturbing the <a href="/wiki/Soil" title="Soil">soil</a> through <a href="/wiki/Tillage" title="Tillage">tillage</a>. No-till farming decreases the amount of <a href="/wiki/Soil_erosion" title="Soil erosion">soil erosion</a> tillage causes in certain soils, especially in sandy and dry soils on sloping terrain. Other possible benefits include an increase in the amount of water that infiltrates the soil, soil retention of organic matter, and <a href="/wiki/Nutrient_cycling" class="mw-redirect" title="Nutrient cycling">nutrient cycling</a>. These methods may increase the amount and variety of life in and on the soil. While conventional no-tillage systems use <a href="/wiki/Herbicide" title="Herbicide">herbicides</a> to control weeds, organic systems use a combination of strategies, such as planting <a href="/wiki/Cover_crops" class="mw-redirect" title="Cover crops">cover crops</a> as mulch to suppress weeds.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:NRCSMD83008_-_Maryland_(4535)(NRCS_Photo_Gallery).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Young soybean plants are being planted in long rows" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/NRCSMD83008_-_Maryland_%284535%29%28NRCS_Photo_Gallery%29.jpg/330px-NRCSMD83008_-_Maryland_%284535%29%28NRCS_Photo_Gallery%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="330" height="236" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/NRCSMD83008_-_Maryland_%284535%29%28NRCS_Photo_Gallery%29.jpg/500px-NRCSMD83008_-_Maryland_%284535%29%28NRCS_Photo_Gallery%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/NRCSMD83008_-_Maryland_%284535%29%28NRCS_Photo_Gallery%29.jpg/960px-NRCSMD83008_-_Maryland_%284535%29%28NRCS_Photo_Gallery%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2100" data-file-height="1500"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="brown rust" term="brown rust" wikidataID="Q100683084" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_rust" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: brown rust<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_rust">Brown rust</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Wheat leaf rust</b> (<i><b>Puccinia triticina</b></i>) is a fungal disease that affects <a href="/wiki/Wheat" title="Wheat">wheat</a>, <a href="/wiki/Barley" title="Barley">barley</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rye" title="Rye">rye</a> stems, leaves and grains. In <a href="/wiki/Temperate_zones" class="mw-redirect" title="Temperate zones">temperate zones</a> it is destructive on <a href="/wiki/Winter_wheat" title="Winter wheat">winter wheat</a> because the pathogen <a href="/wiki/Overwinter" class="mw-redirect" title="Overwinter">overwinters</a>. Infections can lead up to 20% <a href="/wiki/Crop_yield" title="Crop yield">yield</a> loss. The pathogen is a <i><a href="/wiki/Puccinia" title="Puccinia">Puccinia</a></i> <a href="/wiki/Rust_(fungus)" title="Rust (fungus)">rust fungus</a>. It is the most prevalent of all the wheat rust diseases, occurring in most wheat-growing regions.<sup id="cite_ref-Liu-et-al-2013_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Liu-et-al-2013-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It causes serious <a href="/wiki/Epidemic" title="Epidemic">epidemics</a> in <a href="/wiki/North_America" title="North America">North America</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mexico" title="Mexico">Mexico</a> and <a href="/wiki/South_America" title="South America">South America</a> and is a devastating seasonal disease in <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a>. <i>P. triticina</i> is <a href="/wiki/Heteroecious" title="Heteroecious">heteroecious</a>, requiring two distinct hosts (alternate hosts).<sup id="cite_ref-Liu-et-al-2013_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Liu-et-al-2013-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Bolton-et-al-2008_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bolton-et-al-2008-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<p></p></div><div name="broccoli" term="broccoli" wikidataID="Q47722" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broccoli" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: broccoli<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broccoli">Broccoli</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Broccoli</b> (<i><a href="/wiki/Brassica_oleracea" title="Brassica oleracea">Brassica oleracea</a></i> var. <i>italica</i>) is an edible green plant in the <a href="/wiki/Brassicaceae" title="Brassicaceae">cabbage family</a> (family Brassicaceae, genus <i>Brassica</i>) whose large <a href="/wiki/Pseudanthium" title="Pseudanthium">flowering head</a>, <a href="/wiki/Plant_stem" title="Plant stem">stalk</a> and small associated <a href="/wiki/Leafy_greens" class="mw-redirect" title="Leafy greens">leaves</a> are eaten as a <a href="/wiki/Vegetable" title="Vegetable">vegetable</a>. Broccoli is classified in the <a href="/wiki/Brassica_oleracea#Cultivar_groups" title="Brassica oleracea">Italica</a> <a href="/wiki/Cultivar_group" title="Cultivar group">cultivar group</a> of the species <i><a href="/wiki/Brassica_oleracea" title="Brassica oleracea">Brassica oleracea</a></i>. Broccoli has large <a href="/wiki/Flower_head" class="mw-redirect" title="Flower head">flower heads</a>, or florets, usually dark green, arranged in a tree-like structure branching out from a thick <a href="/wiki/Plant_stem" title="Plant stem">stalk</a>, which is usually light green. Leaves surround the mass of flower heads. Broccoli resembles <a href="/wiki/Cauliflower" title="Cauliflower">cauliflower</a>, a different but closely related cultivar group of the same <i>Brassica</i> species.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Broccoli_plants_growing_in_New_Jersey_in_April.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Broccoli_plants_growing_in_New_Jersey_in_April.jpg/250px-Broccoli_plants_growing_in_New_Jersey_in_April.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="183" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Broccoli_plants_growing_in_New_Jersey_in_April.jpg/500px-Broccoli_plants_growing_in_New_Jersey_in_April.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="988" data-file-height="725"></a><figcaption>Broccoli plants in a nursery</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="breeding program" term="breeding program" wikidataID="Q4960291" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breeding_program" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: breeding program<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breeding_program">Breeding program</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">A <b>breeding program</b> is the planned <a href="/wiki/Selective_breeding" title="Selective breeding">breeding</a> of a group of <a href="/wiki/Animal" title="Animal">animals</a> or <a href="/wiki/Plant" title="Plant">plants</a>, usually involving at least several individuals and extending over several <a href="/wiki/Generation" title="Generation">generations</a>. There are a couple of breeding methods, such as artificial (which is man made) and natural (it occurs on its own).
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Entrance_De_Wildt_Cheetah_Research_Centre,_South_Africa.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Entrance_De_Wildt_Cheetah_Research_Centre%2C_South_Africa.jpg/250px-Entrance_De_Wildt_Cheetah_Research_Centre%2C_South_Africa.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="166" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Entrance_De_Wildt_Cheetah_Research_Centre%2C_South_Africa.jpg/500px-Entrance_De_Wildt_Cheetah_Research_Centre%2C_South_Africa.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3696" data-file-height="2448"></a><figcaption>Entrance of <i><a href="/wiki/De_Wildt_Cheetah_and_Wildlife_Centre" title="De Wildt Cheetah and Wildlife Centre">De Wildt Cheetah and Wildlife Centre</a></i> in <a href="/wiki/South_Africa" title="South Africa">South Africa</a>. Breeding programs play a role in the conservation and preservation of the <a href="/wiki/Cheetah" title="Cheetah">cheetah</a> and the <a href="/wiki/African_wild_dog" title="African wild dog">African wild dog</a></figcaption></figure>

The annual recurrence of stem rust of wheat in North Indian plains was discovered by K. C. Mehta.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Since the 1950s, wheat strains bred to be resistant to stem rust have become available.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Fungicide" title="Fungicide">Fungicides</a> effective against stem rust are available as well.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

You can <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_wizard" title="Wikipedia:Article wizard">create a draft and submit it for review</a> or <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_creation/Redirects" title="Wikipedia:Articles for creation/Redirects">request that a redirect be created</a>, but consider checking the search results below to see whether the topic is already covered.</i></p><p></p></div><div name="cottonseed" term="cottonseed" wikidataID="Q17104079" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottonseed" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: cottonseed<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottonseed">Cottonseed</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Cottonseed</b> is the <a href="/wiki/Seed" title="Seed">seed</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Cotton_plant" class="mw-redirect" title="Cotton plant">cotton plant</a>, formed inside the <a href="/wiki/Cotton_boll" class="mw-redirect" title="Cotton boll">cotton boll</a>. Cottonseed is the source of <a href="/wiki/Cottonseed_oil" title="Cottonseed oil">cottonseed oil</a> and <b>cottonseed meal</b>. Cottonseed, like the rest of the cotton plant, contains high amounts of <a href="/wiki/Gossypol" title="Gossypol">gossypol</a> that can be toxic to humans. Cottonseed has been historically used as an <a href="/wiki/Ersatz" class="mw-redirect" title="Ersatz">ersatz</a> <a href="/wiki/Protein_(nutrient)#Sources" title="Protein (nutrient)">protein-rich food</a> in cotton-producing regions, but the modern <a href="/wiki/Biofortification" title="Biofortification">biofortification</a> of cotton <a href="/wiki/Cultivars" class="mw-redirect" title="Cultivars">cultivars</a> with tolerable gossypol levels has particular relevance to <a href="/wiki/Cotton#Fair_trade" title="Cotton">impoverished cotton producers</a>.
</p>
<div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cotton_seeds_-_01.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Cotton_seeds_-_01.jpg/250px-Cotton_seeds_-_01.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="181" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Cotton_seeds_-_01.jpg/500px-Cotton_seeds_-_01.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="690" data-file-height="500"></a><figcaption>Cottonseed: brown seeds are <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/en:gin#Verb" class="extiw" title="wikt:en:gin">ginned</a> from the <a href="/wiki/Plant_fiber" class="mw-redirect" title="Plant fiber">fiber</a> <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/boll" class="extiw" title="wikt:boll">boll</a>; white seeds are still wrapped in <a href="/wiki/Cotton_linters" class="mw-redirect" title="Cotton linters">cotton linters</a></figcaption></figure>
