The term is also used to describe <a href="/wiki/Bacillus_(shape)" class="mw-redirect" title="Bacillus (shape)">the shape (rod)</a> of other so-shaped bacteria; and the plural <i>Bacilli</i> is the name of the <a href="/wiki/Class_(biology)" title="Class (biology)">class</a> of bacteria to which this genus belongs. <i>Bacillus</i> species can be either <a href="/wiki/Obligate_aerobe" title="Obligate aerobe">obligate aerobes</a> which are dependent on <a href="/wiki/Oxygen" title="Oxygen">oxygen</a>, or <a href="/wiki/Facultative_anaerobes" class="mw-redirect" title="Facultative anaerobes">facultative anaerobes</a> which can survive in the absence of oxygen. Cultured <i>Bacillus</i> species test positive for the <a href="/wiki/Enzyme" title="Enzyme">enzyme</a> <a href="/wiki/Catalase" title="Catalase">catalase</a> if oxygen has been used or is present.<sup id="cite_ref-Turnbull_1996_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Turnbull_1996-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

href="/wiki/Bacterium" class="mw-redirect" title="Bacterium">bacterium</a>, and is the most commonly used <a href="/wiki/Biological_pesticide" class="mw-redirect" title="Biological pesticide">biological pesticide</a> worldwide. <i>B. thuringiensis</i> also occurs naturally in the gut of <a href="/wiki/Caterpillar" title="Caterpillar">caterpillars</a> of various types of <a href="/wiki/Moth" title="Moth">moths</a> and <a href="/wiki/Butterfly" title="Butterfly">butterflies</a>, as well as on leaf surfaces, aquatic environments, animal feces, insect-rich environments, flour mills and grain-storage facilities.<sup id="cite_ref-Brock_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brock-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spodoptera_litura" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Spodoptera litura<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spodoptera_litura">Spodoptera litura</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><i><b>Spodoptera litura</b></i>, otherwise known as the <b>tobacco cutworm</b> or <b>cotton leafworm</b>, is a nocturnal <a href="/wiki/Moth" title="Moth">moth</a> in the family <a href="/wiki/Noctuidae" title="Noctuidae">Noctuidae</a>. <i>S. litura</i> is a serious <a href="/wiki/Polyphagous" class="mw-redirect" title="Polyphagous">polyphagous</a> pest in <a href="/wiki/Asia" title="Asia">Asia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Oceania" title="Oceania">Oceania</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</a> that was first described by <a href="/wiki/Johan_Christian_Fabricius" title="Johan Christian Fabricius">Johan Christian Fabricius</a> in 1775.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Its common names reference two of the most frequent host plants of the moth. In total, 87 species of host plants that are infested by <i>S. litura</i> are of economic importance.<sup id="cite_ref-:8_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:8-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The species parasitize the plants as larvae through vigorous eating patterns, oftentimes leaving the leaves completely destroyed. The moth destroys economically important agricultural crops and decreases yield in some plants completely.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Their potential impact on the many different cultivated crops, and subsequently the local agricultural economy, has led to serious efforts to control the pests.<sup id="cite_ref-:10_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:10-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Spodoptera_litura_(24045593674).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Spodoptera_litura_%2824045593674%29.jpg/250px-Spodoptera_litura_%2824045593674%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Spodoptera_litura_%2824045593674%29.jpg/500px-Spodoptera_litura_%2824045593674%29.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="5472" data-file-height="3648"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="oil yield" term="oil yield" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=oil%20yield" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: oil yield<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=oil%20yield">oil yield</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">

Africa<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa">South Africa</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>South Africa</b>, officially the <b>Republic of South Africa</b> (<b>RSA</b>), is the <a href="/wiki/Southern_Africa" title="Southern Africa">southernmost</a> country in <a href="/wiki/Africa" title="Africa">Africa</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>d<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Its <a href="/wiki/Provinces_of_South_Africa" title="Provinces of South Africa">nine provinces</a> are bounded to the south by 2,798 kilometres (1,739 miles) of <a href="/wiki/Coastline" class="mw-redirect" title="Coastline">coastline</a> that stretches along the <a href="/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean" title="Atlantic Ocean">South Atlantic</a> and <a href="/wiki/Indian_Ocean" title="Indian Ocean">Indian Ocean</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-safacts_23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-safacts-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> to the north by the neighbouring countries of <a href="/wiki/Namibia" title="Namibia">Namibia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Botswana" title="Botswana">Botswana</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Zimbabwe" title="Zimbabwe">Zimbabwe</a>; to the east and northeast by <a href="/wiki/Mozambique" title="Mozambique">Mozambique</a> and <a href="/wiki/Eswatini" title="Eswatini">Eswatini</a>; and it encloses <a href="/wiki/Lesotho" title="Lesotho">Lesotho</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Covering an area of 1,221,037 square kilometres (471,445 square miles), the country has <a href="/wiki/Demographics_of_South_Africa" title="Demographics of South Africa">a population</a> of over 63 million people, making it the <a href="/wiki/List_of_African_countries_by_population" title="List of African countries by population">sixth-most populated country</a> in Africa. <a href="/wiki/Pretoria" title="Pretoria">Pretoria</a> is the administrative capital, while <a href="/wiki/Cape_Town" title="Cape Town">Cape Town</a>, as the seat of <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_South_Africa" title="Parliament of South Africa">Parliament</a>, is the legislative capital, and <a href="/wiki/Bloemfontein" title="Bloemfontein">Bloemfontein</a> is regarded as the judicial capital.<sup id="cite_ref-Marais_Twala_2020_pp._49&#8211;62_25-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Marais_Twala_2020_pp._49%E2%80%9362-25"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The largest and most populous city is <a href="/wiki/Johannesburg" title="Johannesburg">Johannesburg</a>, followed by Cape Town and <a href="/wiki/Durban" title="Durban">Durban</a>.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Maropeng_visitor_centre,_Cradle_of_Humankind,_South_Africa.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Maropeng_visitor_centre%2C_Cradle_of_Humankind%2C_South_Africa.jpg/250px-Maropeng_visitor_centre%2C_Cradle_of_Humankind%2C_South_Africa.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="145" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Maropeng_visitor_centre%2C_Cradle_of_Humankind%2C_South_Africa.jpg/500px-Maropeng_visitor_centre%2C_Cradle_of_Humankind%2C_South_Africa.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3523" data-file-height="2042"></a><figcaption>Front of Maropeng at the <a href="/wiki/Cradle_of_Humankind" title="Cradle of Humankind">Cradle of Humankind</a></figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="Rights" term="Rights" wikidataID="Q780687" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rights" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Rights<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rights">Rights</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Rights</b> are <a href="/wiki/Law" title="Law">legal</a>, social, or <a href="/wiki/Ethics" title="Ethics">ethical</a> <a href="/wiki/Principle" title="Principle">principles</a> of <a href="/wiki/Freedom" title="Freedom">freedom</a> or <a href="/wiki/Entitlement_(fair_division)" title="Entitlement (fair division)">entitlement</a>; that is, rights are the fundamental <a href="/wiki/Normative" class="mw-redirect" title="Normative">normative</a> rules about what is allowed of people or owed to people according to some legal system, <a href="/wiki/Social_convention" class="mw-redirect" title="Social convention">social convention</a>, or ethical theory.<sup id="cite_ref-tws21decgghg_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tws21decgghg-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Rights are an important concept in <a href="/wiki/Law" title="Law">law</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ethics" title="Ethics">ethics</a>, especially theories of <a href="/wiki/Justice" title="Justice">justice</a> and <a href="/wiki/Deontology" title="Deontology">deontology</a>.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Brueghel_Jan_II_God_creating.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="painting of dark gray skies with trees and water, and a human image, flying, with arms outstretched" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Brueghel_Jan_II_God_creating.jpg/250px-Brueghel_Jan_II_God_creating.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="198" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Brueghel_Jan_II_God_creating.jpg/500px-Brueghel_Jan_II_God_creating.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="799" data-file-height="633"></a><figcaption>According to some views, certain rights derive from <a href="/wiki/Deities" class="mw-redirect" title="Deities">deities</a> or <a href="/wiki/Nature" title="Nature">nature</a>.</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="PPVFR Act" term="PPVFR Act" wikidataID="Q7251349" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PPVFR_Act" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: PPVFR Act<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PPVFR_Act">PPVFR Act</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">The <b>Protection of Plant Variety and Farmers Right Act, 2001</b> (<b>PPVFR Act</b>) is an <a href="/wiki/Act_of_Parliament" class="mw-redirect" title="Act of Parliament">Act</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_India" title="Parliament of India">Parliament of India</a> granting intellectual property rights to plant breeders, researchers and farmers who develop new or extant plant varieties. This act received the assent of the <a href="/wiki/President_of_India" title="President of India">President of India</a> on the 30 October 2001.
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Emblem_of_India.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Emblem_of_India.svg/250px-Emblem_of_India.svg.png" decoding="async" width="150" height="239" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Emblem_of_India.svg/330px-Emblem_of_India.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="550" data-file-height="877"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="endophytes" term="endophytes" wikidataID="Q260335" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endophytes" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: endophytes<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endophytes">Endophytes</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">An <b>endophyte</b> is an <a href="/wiki/Endosymbiont" title="Endosymbiont">endosymbiont</a>, often a <a href="/wiki/Bacterium" class="mw-redirect" title="Bacterium">bacterium</a> or <a href="/wiki/Fungus" title="Fungus">fungus</a>, that lives within a <a href="/wiki/Plant" title="Plant">plant</a> for at least part of its life cycle without causing apparent disease. Endophytes are ubiquitous and have been found in all species of plants studied to date; however, most of the endophyte/plant relationships are not well understood. Some endophytes may enhance host growth and nutrient acquisition and improve the plant's ability to tolerate abiotic stresses, such as drought, and decrease biotic stresses by enhancing plant resistance to insects, pathogens and <a href="/wiki/Herbivore" title="Herbivore">herbivores</a>. Although endophytic bacteria and fungi are frequently studied, endophytic archaea are increasingly being considered for their role in plant growth promotion as part of the core microbiome of a plant.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Root-nodule01.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Root-nodule01.jpg/250px-Root-nodule01.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="185" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Root-nodule01.jpg/500px-Root-nodule01.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2240" data-file-height="1654"></a><figcaption>Transmission electron microscope image of a cross section through a soybean (<i><a href="/wiki/Glycine_max" class="mw-redirect" title="Glycine max">Glycine max</a></i>) <a href="/wiki/Root_nodule" title="Root nodule">root nodule</a>. The nitrogen fixing bacteria, and fungi <i><a href="/wiki/Bradyrhizobium_japonicum" title="Bradyrhizobium japonicum">Bradyrhizobium japonicum</a></i>, infects the roots and establishes a symbiosis. This high magnification image shows part of a cell with single bacteroid (bacterium-like cell or modified bacterial cell) within their <a href="/wiki/Symbiosome" title="Symbiosome">symbiosomes</a>. In this image, you can also see <a href="/wiki/Endoplasmic_reticulum" title="Endoplasmic reticulum">endoplasmic reticulum</a>, <a href="/wiki/Golgi_apparatus" title="Golgi apparatus">Golgi apparatus</a> and cell wall.</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="fertigation" term="fertigation" wikidataID="Q1408226" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertigation" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: fertigation<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertigation">Fertigation</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Fertigation</b> is the <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/injection" class="extiw" title="wikt:injection">injection</a> of <a href="/wiki/Fertilizers" class="mw-redirect" title="Fertilizers">fertilizers</a>, used for <a href="/wiki/Soil_amendments" class="mw-redirect" title="Soil amendments">soil amendments</a>, water amendments and other <a href="/wiki/Water" title="Water">water</a>-<a href="/wiki/Solubility" title="Solubility">soluble</a> products into an <a href="/wiki/Irrigation" title="Irrigation">irrigation</a> system.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Polibeg_putih_fertigasi_2.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Polibeg_putih_fertigasi_2.JPG/250px-Polibeg_putih_fertigasi_2.JPG" decoding="async" width="190" height="253" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Polibeg_putih_fertigasi_2.JPG/330px-Polibeg_putih_fertigasi_2.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Polibeg_putih_fertigasi_2.JPG/500px-Polibeg_putih_fertigasi_2.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1944" data-file-height="2592"></a><figcaption>Fertigation using white poly bag</figcaption></figure>

id="cite_ref-WU_2020_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WU_2020-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Viruses infect all <a class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Since <a href="/wiki/Dmitri_Ivanovsky" title="Dmitri Ivanovsky">Dmitri Ivanovsky</a>'s 1892 article describing a non-bacterial <a href="/wiki/Pathogen" class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 4">:&#8202;4&#8202;</span></sup> more than 16,000 of the millions of <a href="/wiki/Virus_species" class="mw-redirect" title="Virus species">virus species</a> have been described in detail.<sup id="cite_ref-ictv_2024_7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ictv_2024-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Breitbart_2005_8-0" class="reference"><a Fukuoka, a Japanese <a href="/wiki/Farmer" title="Farmer">farmer</a> and philosopher, introduced the term in his 1975 book <i><a href="/wiki/The_One-Straw_Revolution" class="mw-redirect" title="The One-Straw Revolution">The One-Straw Revolution</a></i>. The title refers not to lack of effort, but to the avoidance of manufactured inputs and equipment. Natural farming is related to fertility farming, <a href="/wiki/Organic_farming" title="Organic farming">organic farming</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sustainable_agriculture" title="Sustainable agriculture">sustainable agriculture</a>, <a href="/wiki/Agroecology" title="Agroecology">agroecology</a>, <a href="/wiki/Agroforestry" title="Agroforestry">agroforestry</a>, <a href="/wiki/Landscape-scale_conservation#Ecoagriculture" title="Landscape-scale conservation">ecoagriculture</a> and <a href="/wiki/Permaculture" title="Permaculture">permaculture</a>, but should be distinguished from <a href="/wiki/Biodynamic_agriculture" title="Biodynamic agriculture">biodynamic agriculture</a>.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Masanobu-Fukuoka.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Masanobu-Fukuoka.jpg/250px-Masanobu-Fukuoka.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="241" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fa/Masanobu-Fukuoka.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="481"></a><figcaption>Masanobu Fukuoka, originator of the natural farming method</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="Plant Tissue Culture" term="Plant Tissue Culture" wikidataID="Q1549003" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_tissue_culture" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Plant Tissue Culture<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_tissue_culture">Plant tissue culture</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Plant tissue culture</b> is a collection of techniques used to maintain or grow plant cells, tissues, or organs under sterile conditions on a nutrient culture medium of known composition. It is widely used to produce clones of a plant in a method known as <a href="/wiki/Micropropagation" title="Micropropagation">micropropagation</a>. Different techniques in plant tissue culture may offer certain advantages over traditional methods of propagation, including:</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Plant_Tissue_culture.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ad/Plant_Tissue_culture.jpg" decoding="async" width="211" height="155" class="mw-file-element" data-file-width="211" data-file-height="155"></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/In_vitro" title="In vitro">In vitro</a></i> tissue culture of potato <a href="/wiki/Explant" class="mw-redirect" title="Explant">explants</a></figcaption></figure>

It is a reddish-brown liquid. The chemical formula is C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>15</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>PS, and IUPAC name <i>O</i>,<i>O</i>-diethyl <i>O</i>-quinoxalin-2-yl phosphorothioate.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Ranked 'moderately hazardous' in <a href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</a>'s (WHO) acute hazard ranking, use of quinalphos, classified as a <a href="/wiki/Yellow_label" class="mw-redirect" title="Yellow label">yellow label</a> (highly toxic) pesticide in <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a>, is widely used in the following crops: <a href="/wiki/Wheat" title="Wheat">wheat</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rice" title="Rice">rice</a>, <a href="/wiki/Coffee" title="Coffee">coffee</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sugarcane" title="Sugarcane">sugarcane</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Cotton" title="Cotton">cotton</a>.
</p>

It is widely cultivated as a crop for human consumption, and also as a <a href="/wiki/Cover_crop" title="Cover crop">cover crop</a>. Varieties with smaller, harder seeds that are fed to horses or other animals are called <b>field bean</b>, <b>tic bean</b> or <b>tick bean</b>. This <a href="/wiki/Legume" title="Legume">legume</a> is commonly consumed in many national and regional cuisines.

These organisms are classified in the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_(biology)" title="Kingdom (biology)">kingdom</a> <b>Fungi</b>.<sup id="cite_ref-Whittaker1969_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Whittaker1969-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-CavalierSmith1998_13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CavalierSmith1998-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Fungi_collage.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A collage of five fungi (clockwise from top left): a mushroom with a flat red top with white spots and a white stem growing on the ground; a red cup-shaped fungus growing on wood; a stack of green and white moldy bread slices on a plate; a microscopic spherical grey semitransparent cell with a smaller spherical cell beside it; a microscopic view of an elongated cellular structure shaped like a microphone, attached to the larger end is a number of smaller roughly circular elements that collectively form a mass around it" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Fungi_collage.jpg/330px-Fungi_collage.jpg" decoding="async" width="330" height="287" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Fungi_collage.jpg/500px-Fungi_collage.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Fungi_collage.jpg/960px-Fungi_collage.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1220" data-file-height="1062"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="rBiFC vectors" term="rBiFC vectors" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=rBiFC%20vectors" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: rBiFC vectors<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=rBiFC%20vectors">rBiFC vectors</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">

This occurs due to excessive standing water around the roots.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It is found in both indoor and outdoor plants, although it is more common in indoor plants due to overwatering, heavy potting media, or containers with poor <a href="/wiki/Drainage" class="mw-redirect" title="Drainage">drainage</a>. The leaves of plants experiencing root rot often yellow and die, and if allowed to continue, the condition can be fatal to the plant.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Root_rot_in_cicer_arietinum_(hydro-grown).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Chickpea with root rot" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Root_rot_in_cicer_arietinum_%28hydro-grown%29.jpg/250px-Root_rot_in_cicer_arietinum_%28hydro-grown%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="634" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Root_rot_in_cicer_arietinum_%28hydro-grown%29.jpg/500px-Root_rot_in_cicer_arietinum_%28hydro-grown%29.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="808" data-file-height="2048"></a><figcaption>Chickpea plant (<i><a href="/wiki/Chickpea" title="Chickpea">Cicer arietinum</a></i>) with root rot. Note the symptomatic discolouration in some of its leaves.</figcaption></figure>

You can <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_wizard" title="Wikipedia:Article wizard">create a draft and submit it for review</a> or <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_creation/Redirects" title="Wikipedia:Articles for creation/Redirects">request that a redirect be created</a>, but consider checking the search results below to see whether the topic is already covered.</i></p><p></p></div><div name="soil management" term="soil management" wikidataID="Q7554944" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_management" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: soil management<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_management">Soil management</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Soil management</b> is the application of operations, practices, and treatments to protect <a href="/wiki/Soil" title="Soil">soil</a> and enhance its performance (such as <a href="/wiki/Soil_fertility" title="Soil fertility">soil fertility</a> or <a href="/wiki/Soil_mechanics" title="Soil mechanics">soil mechanics</a>). It includes <a href="/wiki/Soil_conservation" title="Soil conservation">soil conservation</a>, <a href="/wiki/Soil_conditioner" title="Soil conditioner">soil amendment</a>, and optimal <a href="/wiki/Soil_health" title="Soil health">soil health</a>. In <a href="/wiki/Agriculture" title="Agriculture">agriculture</a>, some amount of soil management is needed both in nonorganic and <a href="/wiki/Organic_farming" title="Organic farming">organic</a> types to prevent <a href="/wiki/Agricultural_land" title="Agricultural land">agricultural land</a> from becoming less productive over decades. Organic farming in particular emphasizes more on optimal soil management, because it uses soil health as the exclusive or nearly exclusive source of its <a href="/wiki/Fertilizer" title="Fertilizer">fertilization</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pest_control" title="Pest control">pest control</a>.
</p><div title="figure"><figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Palau_taro_patch_soil_management.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Palau_taro_patch_soil_management.jpg/330px-Palau_taro_patch_soil_management.jpg" decoding="async" width="315" height="236" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Palau_taro_patch_soil_management.jpg/500px-Palau_taro_patch_soil_management.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Palau_taro_patch_soil_management.jpg/960px-Palau_taro_patch_soil_management.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1500" data-file-height="1125"></a><figcaption>Cover cropping and mulching practiced as soil management in Palau</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="water stress" term="water stress" wikidataID="Q5376358" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_stress" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: water stress<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_stress">Water stress</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Water scarcity</b> (closely related to <b>water stress</b> or <a href="/wiki/Water_crisis_(disambiguation)" class="mw-redirect mw-disambig" title="Water crisis (disambiguation)">water crisis</a>) is the lack of any, local or economically viably transportable, sources of <a href="/wiki/Fresh_water" title="Fresh water">fresh water</a> <a href="/wiki/Water_resources" title="Water resources">resources</a> to meet the standard water demand in a region. There are two types of water scarcity. One is <i>physical.</i> The other is <i>economic water scarcity</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-Caretta-2022a_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Caretta-2022a-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 560">:&#8202;560&#8202;</span></sup> Physical water scarcity is where there is not enough water to meet all demands. This includes water needed for <a href="/wiki/Ecosystem" title="Ecosystem">ecosystems</a> to function. Regions with a <a href="/wiki/Desert_climate" title="Desert climate">desert climate</a> often face physical water scarcity.<sup id="cite_ref-Rijsberman-2006a_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Rijsberman-2006a-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Central_Asia" title="Central Asia">Central Asia</a>, <a href="/wiki/West_Asia" title="West Asia">West Asia</a>, and <a href="/wiki/North_Africa" title="North Africa">North Africa</a> are examples of arid areas. Economic water scarcity results from a lack of investment in infrastructure or technology to draw water from rivers, <a href="/wiki/Aquifer" title="Aquifer">aquifers</a>, or other water sources. It also results from weak human capacity to meet water demand.<sup id="cite_ref-Caretta-2022a_2-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Caretta-2022a-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 560">:&#8202;560&#8202;</span></sup> Many people in <a href="/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa" title="Sub-Saharan Africa">sub-Saharan Africa</a> are living with economic water scarcity.<sup id="cite_ref-IWMI-2007_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-IWMI-2007-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 11">:&#8202;11&#8202;</span></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Water_stress_2019_WRI.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Water_stress_2019_WRI.png/330px-Water_stress_2019_WRI.png" decoding="async" width="300" height="132" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Water_stress_2019_WRI.png/500px-Water_stress_2019_WRI.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Water_stress_2019_WRI.png/960px-Water_stress_2019_WRI.png 2x" data-file-width="1425" data-file-height="625"></a><figcaption>Map of global water stress (a symptom of water scarcity) in 2019. Water stress is the ratio of water use relative to water availability and is therefore a demand-driven scarcity.<sup id="cite_ref-Kummu-2016_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Kummu-2016-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="gray mold" term="gray mold" wikidataID="Q1135851" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gray_mold" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: gray mold<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gray_mold">Gray mold</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><i><b>Botrytis cinerea</b></i> is a <a href="/wiki/Necrotrophic" class="mw-redirect" title="Necrotrophic">necrotrophic</a> <a href="/wiki/Fungus" title="Fungus">fungus</a> that affects many plant species, including <a href="/wiki/List_of_grape_varieties" title="List of grape varieties">wine grapes</a>. Development<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_Development">Sustainable Development</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Sustainable development</b> is an approach to growth and <a href="/wiki/Human_development_(economics)" title="Human development (economics)">human development</a> that aims to meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:72_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:72-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The aim is to have a society where living conditions and resources meet human needs without undermining <a href="/wiki/Planetary_integrity" class="mw-redirect" title="Planetary integrity">planetary integrity</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Sustainable development aims to balance the needs of the <a href="/wiki/Economic_development" title="Economic development">economy</a>, <a href="/wiki/Environmental_protection" title="Environmental protection">environment</a>, and society. Sustainable development aims to balance the needs of the economy, environment, and society. Equitable health access is a pillar of social sustainability. The <a href="/wiki/Brundtland_Report" class="mw-redirect" title="Brundtland Report">Brundtland Report</a> in 1987 helped to make the concept of sustainable development better known.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Visualization_of_pillars_of_sustainability.webp" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Visualization_of_pillars_of_sustainability.webp/250px-Visualization_of_pillars_of_sustainability.webp.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="159" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Visualization_of_pillars_of_sustainability.webp/500px-Visualization_of_pillars_of_sustainability.webp.png 1.5x" data-file-width="869" data-file-height="553"></a><figcaption>Three visual representations of sustainability and its three dimensions. It is commonly called <b>ricebean</b> or <b>rice bean</b>. To date, it is little known, little researched, and little exploited.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It is regarded as a minor <a href="/wiki/Food" title="Food">food</a> and <a href="/wiki/Fodder" title="Fodder">fodder</a> crop and is often grown as <a href="/wiki/Intercrop" class="mw-redirect" title="Intercrop">intercrop</a> or mixed crop with <a href="/wiki/Maize" title="Maize">maize</a> (<i>Zea mays</i>), <a href="/wiki/Sorghum" title="Sorghum">sorghum</a> (<i><a href="/wiki/Sorghum_bicolor" class="mw-redirect" title="Sorghum bicolor">Sorghum bicolor</a></i>) or <a href="/wiki/Cowpea" title="Cowpea">cowpea</a> (<i>V. unguiculata</i>), as well as a sole crop in the uplands, on a very limited area. Like the other Asiatic <i><a href="/wiki/Vigna" title="Vigna">Vigna</a></i> species, ricebean is a fairly short-lived warm-season annual. Grown mainly as a dried <a href="/wiki/Pulse_(legume)" class="mw-redirect" title="Pulse (legume)">pulse</a>, it is also important as a fodder, a <a href="/wiki/Green_manure" title="Green manure">green manure</a> and a vegetable. Ricebean is most widely grown as an <a href="/wiki/Intercrop" class="mw-redirect" title="Intercrop">intercrop</a>, particularly of maize, throughout <a href="/wiki/Indo-China" class="mw-redirect" title="Indo-China">Indo-China</a> and extending into southern <a href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</a>, <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nepal" title="Nepal">Nepal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh" title="Bangladesh">Bangladesh</a>. In the past it was widely grown as lowland crop on residual soil water after the harvest of long-season <a href="/wiki/Rice" title="Rice">rice</a>, but it has been displaced to a great extent where shorter duration rice varieties are grown. Ricebean grows well on a range of soils. It establishes rapidly and has the potential to produce large amounts of nutritious animal fodder and high quality grain.
</p>

A BCR is the ratio of the benefits of a project or proposal, expressed in monetary terms, relative to its costs, also expressed in monetary terms. All benefits and costs should be expressed in discounted <a href="/wiki/Present_value" title="Present value">present values</a>. A BCR can be a <a href="/wiki/Profitability_index" title="Profitability index">profitability index</a> in for-profit contexts. A BCR takes into account the amount of monetary gain realized by performing a project versus the amount it costs to execute the project. The higher the BCR the better the investment. The general rule of thumb is that if the benefit is higher than the cost the project is a good investment.

As well as dating them, this can give data for <a href="/wiki/Dendroclimatology" title="Dendroclimatology">dendroclimatology</a>, the study of climate and atmospheric conditions during different periods in history from the wood of old trees. Dendrochronology derives from the Ancient Greek <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language romanization"><i lang="grc-Latn">dendron</i></span> (<span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc"><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%CE%B4%CE%AD%CE%BD%CE%B4%CF%81%CE%BF%CE%BD" class="extiw" title="wikt:&#948;&#941;&#957;&#948;&#961;&#959;&#957;">&#948;&#941;&#957;&#948;&#961;&#959;&#957;</a></span></span>), meaning "tree", <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language romanization"><i lang="grc-Latn">khronos</i></span> (<span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc"><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%CF%87%CF%81%CF%8C%CE%BD%CE%BF%CF%82" class="extiw" title="wikt:&#967;&#961;&#972;&#957;&#959;&#962;">&#967;&#961;&#972;&#957;&#959;&#962;</a></span></span>), meaning "time", and <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language romanization"><i lang="grc-Latn"><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/-logia" class="extiw" title="wikt:-logia">-logia</a></i></span> (<span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text"><span lang="grc"><a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/-%CE%BB%CE%BF%CE%B3%CE%AF%CE%B1" class="extiw" title="wikt:-&#955;&#959;&#947;&#943;&#945;">-&#955;&#959;&#947;&#943;&#945;</a></span></span>), "the study of".<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Tree.ring.arp.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Tree.ring.arp.jpg/250px-Tree.ring.arp.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="187" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Tree.ring.arp.jpg/500px-Tree.ring.arp.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1800" data-file-height="1347"></a><figcaption>The growth rings of a tree at <a href="/wiki/Bristol_Zoo" title="Bristol Zoo">Bristol Zoo</a>, <a href="/wiki/England" title="England">England</a>. </div><p></p></div><div name="essential oils" term="essential oils" wikidataID="Q170885" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_oils" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: essential oils<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_oils">Essential oils</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Essential oils</b> are compodes of <a href="/wiki/Hydrophobic" class="mw-redirect" title="Hydrophobic">hydrophobic</a> volatile <a href="/wiki/Volatile_organic_compound" title="Volatile organic compound">organic compounds</a>, usually in liquid form, obtained from <a href="/wiki/Plant" title="Plant">plant</a> material. Essential oils are also known as <b>volatile oils</b>, <b>ethereal oils</b>, <b>aetheroleum</b>, or simply as the oil of the plant from which they were extracted, such as <a href="/wiki/Oil_of_clove" title="Oil of clove">oil of clove</a>. An essential <a href="/wiki/Oil" title="Oil">oil</a> is essential in the sense that the oil contains the <a href="/wiki/Fragrance" class="mw-redirect" title="Fragrance">fragrance</a> or essence of the plant.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The term "essential" used here does <i>not</i> indicate that it is nutritionally required in the diet, as with <a href="/wiki/Essential_amino_acid" title="Essential amino acid">essential amino acid</a> or <a href="/wiki/Essential_fatty_acid" title="Essential fatty acid">essential fatty acid</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-halign-center" typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:SandalwoodEssOil.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/SandalwoodEssOil.png/250px-SandalwoodEssOil.png" decoding="async" width="145" height="241" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/SandalwoodEssOil.png/330px-SandalwoodEssOil.png 2x" data-file-width="771" data-file-height="1280"></a><figcaption></figcaption></figure></div><p></p></div><div name="castor hybrid" term="castor hybrid" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=castor%20hybrid" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: castor hybrid<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=castor%20hybrid">castor hybrid</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">

It is widely cultivated as a crop for human consumption, and also as a <a href="/wiki/Cover_crop" title="Cover crop">cover crop</a>. Varieties with smaller, harder seeds that are fed to horses or other animals are called <b>field bean</b>, <b>tic bean</b> or <b>tick bean</b>. Australia is the world's flattest and driest inhabited continent. It is a <a href="/wiki/Megadiverse_countries" title="Megadiverse countries">megadiverse country</a>, and its size gives it a wide variety of landscapes and <a href="/wiki/Climate_of_Australia" title="Climate of Australia">climates</a> including <a href="/wiki/Deserts_of_Australia" title="Deserts of Australia">deserts</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Outback" title="Outback">interior</a> and <a href="/wiki/Forests_of_Australia" title="Forests of Australia">tropical rainforests</a> along the <a href="/wiki/Eastern_states_of_Australia" title="Eastern states of Australia">coast</a>.

Potatoes are underground <a href="/wiki/Tuber#Stem_tuber" title="Tuber">stem tubers</a> of the plant <i><b>Solanum tuberosum</b></i>, a <a href="/wiki/Perennial_plant" class="mw-redirect" title="Perennial plant">perennial</a> in the nightshade family <a href="/wiki/Solanaceae" title="Solanaceae">Solanaceae</a>.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:CIP-Afiche-papa-ingles.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/CIP-Afiche-papa-ingles.jpg/250px-CIP-Afiche-papa-ingles.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="368" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/CIP-Afiche-papa-ingles.jpg/500px-CIP-Afiche-papa-ingles.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="560" data-file-height="825"></a><figcaption>Morphology of the potato plant; <a href="/wiki/Tuber" title="Tuber">tubers</a> are forming from <a href="/wiki/Stolon" title="Stolon">stolons</a>.</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="legumes" term="legumes" wikidataID="Q145909" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legumes" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: legumes<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legumes">Legumes</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Legumes</b> are <a href="/wiki/Plants" class="mw-redirect" title="Plants">plants</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Pea" title="Pea">pea</a> family <a href="/wiki/Fabaceae" title="Fabaceae">Fabaceae</a> (or Leguminosae), or the fruit or seeds of such plants. When used as a dry grain for human consumption, the seeds are also called <b>pulses</b>. Legumes are grown agriculturally, primarily for human consumption, but also as livestock forage and <a href="/wiki/Silage" title="Silage">silage</a>, and as soil-enhancing <a href="/wiki/Green_manure" title="Green manure">green manure</a>. Legumes produce a botanically unique type of <a href="/wiki/Fruit" title="Fruit">fruit</a> &#8211; a <a href="/wiki/Simple_fruit" title="Simple fruit">simple</a> <a href="/wiki/Dry_fruits" title="Dry fruits">dry fruit</a> that develops from a simple <a href="/wiki/Carpel" class="mw-redirect" title="Carpel">carpel</a> and usually <a href="/wiki/Dehiscence_(botany)" title="Dehiscence (botany)">dehisces</a> (opens along a seam) on two sides.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Various_legumes.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Various_legumes.jpg/250px-Various_legumes.jpg" decoding="async" width="230" height="344" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Various_legumes.jpg/500px-Various_legumes.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="957"></a><figcaption>A selection of dried pulses and fresh legumes</figcaption></figure>

</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Spinach_leaves.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Spinach_leaves.jpg/250px-Spinach_leaves.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="185" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Spinach_leaves.jpg/500px-Spinach_leaves.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2439" data-file-height="1800"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Spinach" title="Spinach">Spinach</a> leaves in a <a href="/wiki/Colander" title="Colander">colander</a></figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="leafhoppers" term="leafhoppers" wikidataID="Q244452" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafhoppers" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: leafhoppers<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafhoppers">Leafhoppers</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Leafhopper</b> is the common name for any <a href="/wiki/Species" title="Species">species</a> from the <a href="/wiki/Family_(biology)" title="Family (biology)">family</a> <b>Cicadellidae</b>: based on the <a href="/wiki/Type_genus" title="Type genus">type genus</a> <i><a href="/wiki/Cicadella" title="Cicadella">Cicadella</a></i>. These minute <a href="/wiki/Insect" title="Insect">insects</a>, colloquially known as <b>hoppers</b>, are plant feeders that suck <a href="/wiki/Plant_sap" class="mw-redirect" title="Plant sap">plant sap</a> from grass, shrubs, or trees. Their hind legs are modified for jumping, and are covered with hairs that facilitate the spreading of a secretion over their bodies that acts as a water repellent and carrier of <a href="/wiki/Pheromone" title="Pheromone">pheromones</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Stiller_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stiller-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> They undergo a partial <a href="/wiki/Metamorphosis" title="Metamorphosis">metamorphosis</a>, and have various host associations, varying from very generalized to very specific. Some species have a cosmopolitan distribution, or occur throughout the temperate and tropical regions. Some are pests or <a href="/wiki/Vector_(epidemiology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Vector (epidemiology)">vectors</a> of <a href="/wiki/Plant_virus" title="Plant virus">plant viruses</a> and <a href="/wiki/Phytoplasma" title="Phytoplasma">phytoplasmas</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Stiller_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stiller-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The family is distributed  all over the world, and constitutes the second-largest hemipteran family, with at least 20,000 described species.
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Two-lined_gum_treehopper03.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Two-lined_gum_treehopper03.jpg/250px-Two-lined_gum_treehopper03.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Two-lined_gum_treehopper03.jpg/500px-Two-lined_gum_treehopper03.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1067"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="ricini" term="ricini" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ricini" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: ricini<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ricini">ricini</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">

The family takes its alternative name (Cruciferae, <a href="/wiki/Neo-Latin" title="Neo-Latin">Neo-Latin</a> for "cross-bearing") from the shape of their flowers, whose four <a href="/wiki/Petals" class="mw-redirect" title="Petals">petals</a> resemble a <a href="/wiki/Cross" title="Cross">cross</a>.

</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Opened_garlic_bulb_with_garlic_clove.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Opened_garlic_bulb_with_garlic_clove.jpg/250px-Opened_garlic_bulb_with_garlic_clove.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Opened_garlic_bulb_with_garlic_clove.jpg/500px-Opened_garlic_bulb_with_garlic_clove.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3648" data-file-height="2736"></a><figcaption>Garlic bulb with a removed clove peeled</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="crop production" term="crop production" wikidataID="Q11451" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_production" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: crop production<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_production">Crop production</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Agriculture</b> is the practice of cultivating the soil, planting, raising, and harvesting both food and non-food crops, as well as <a href="/wiki/Livestock" title="Livestock">livestock</a> production. Broader definitions also include <a href="/wiki/Forestry" title="Forestry">forestry</a> and <a href="/wiki/Aquaculture" title="Aquaculture">aquaculture</a>. Agriculture was a key factor in the rise of <a href="/wiki/Sedentism" title="Sedentism">sedentary</a> human <a href="/wiki/Civilization" title="Civilization">civilization</a>, whereby farming of <a href="/wiki/Domestication" title="Domestication">domesticated</a> plants and animals created food <a href="/wiki/Economic_surplus" title="Economic surplus">surpluses</a> that enabled people to live in the cities. While humans started gathering grains at least 105,000 years ago, nascent farmers only began planting them around 11,500 years ago. Sheep, goats, pigs, and cattle were domesticated around 10,000 years ago. Plants were independently cultivated in at least 11 regions of the world. In the 20th century, <a href="/wiki/Industrial_agriculture" title="Industrial agriculture">industrial agriculture</a> based on large-scale <a href="/wiki/Monoculture" title="Monoculture">monocultures</a> came to dominate agricultural output.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:PivotWithDrops.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/PivotWithDrops.JPG/250px-PivotWithDrops.JPG" decoding="async" width="250" height="179" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/PivotWithDrops.JPG/500px-PivotWithDrops.JPG 1.5x" data-file-width="2100" data-file-height="1500"></a><figcaption>Modern agriculture: a <a href="/wiki/Center_pivot_irrigation" class="mw-redirect" title="Center pivot irrigation">center pivot irrigation</a> system on a field</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="crop protection" term="crop protection" wikidataID="Q2306047" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_protection" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: crop protection<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop_protection">Crop protection</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Pest control</b> is the regulation or management of a <a href="/wiki/Species" title="Species">species</a> defined as a <a href="/wiki/Pest_(organism)" title="Pest (organism)">pest</a>; such as any animal, plant or fungus that impacts adversely on human activities or environment.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The human response depends on the importance of the damage done and will range from tolerance, through deterrence and management, to attempts to completely eradicate the pest. Pest control measures may be performed as part of an <a href="/wiki/Integrated_pest_management" title="Integrated pest management">integrated pest management</a> strategy.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Crop_Duster.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Crop_Duster.jpg/500px-Crop_Duster.jpg" decoding="async" width="340" height="432" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Crop_Duster.jpg/960px-Crop_Duster.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1739" data-file-height="2212"></a><figcaption>An <a href="/wiki/Agricultural_aircraft" title="Agricultural aircraft">agricultural aircraft</a> applies low-insecticide bait against <a href="/wiki/Western_corn_rootworm" title="Western corn rootworm">western corn rootworm</a>.</figcaption></figure>

A genome is an organism's complete set of <a href="/wiki/DNA" title="DNA">DNA</a>, including all of its genes as well as its hierarchical, three-dimensional structural configuration.<sup id="cite_ref-Franklin_1953_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Franklin_1953-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Satzinger_2008_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Satzinger_2008-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Cremer_2006_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Cremer_2006-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources#Bundling_citations" title="Wikipedia:Citing sources"><span title="This claim has too many footnotes for reading to be smooth. (November 2024)">excessive citations</span></a></i>]</sup> In contrast to <a href="/wiki/Genetics" title="Genetics">genetics</a>, which refers to the study of <i>individual</i> genes and their roles in inheritance, genomics aims at the collective characterization and quantification of <i>all</i> of an organism's genes, their interrelations and influence on the organism.<sup id="cite_ref-WHO_2004_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WHO_2004-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Genes may direct the production of <a href="/wiki/Proteins" class="mw-redirect" title="Proteins">proteins</a> with the assistance of enzymes and messenger molecules. In turn, proteins make up body structures such as organs and tissues as well as control chemical reactions and carry signals between cells. Genomics also involves the sequencing and analysis of genomes through uses of high throughput <a href="/wiki/DNA_sequencing" title="DNA sequencing">DNA sequencing</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bioinformatics" title="Bioinformatics">bioinformatics</a> to assemble and analyze the function and structure of entire genomes.<sup id="cite_ref-Klug_2012_6-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Klug_2012-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Culver_2002_7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Culver_2002-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Advances in genomics have triggered a revolution in discovery-based research and <a href="/wiki/Systems_biology" title="Systems biology">systems biology</a> to facilitate understanding of even the most complex biological systems such as the brain.<sup id="cite_ref-Kadakkuzha_2013_8-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Kadakkuzha_2013-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Number_of_prokaryotic_genomes_and_sequencing_costs.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt='"Hockey stick" graph showing the exponential growth of public sequence databases.' src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Number_of_prokaryotic_genomes_and_sequencing_costs.svg/330px-Number_of_prokaryotic_genomes_and_sequencing_costs.svg.png" decoding="async" width="300" height="200" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Number_of_prokaryotic_genomes_and_sequencing_costs.svg/500px-Number_of_prokaryotic_genomes_and_sequencing_costs.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Number_of_prokaryotic_genomes_and_sequencing_costs.svg/960px-Number_of_prokaryotic_genomes_and_sequencing_costs.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1350" data-file-height="900"></a><figcaption>The number of genome projects has increased as technological improvements continue to lower the cost of sequencing. <b>(A)</b> Exponential growth of genome sequence databases since 1995. <b>(B)</b> The cost in US Dollars (USD) to sequence one million bases. <b>(C)</b> The cost in USD to sequence a 3,000 Mb (human-sized) genome on a log-transformed scale.</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="grain size" term="grain size" wikidataID="Q466491" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grain_size" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: grain size<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grain_size">Grain size</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Grain size</b> (or <b>particle size</b>) is the <a href="/wiki/Diameter" title="Diameter">diameter</a> of individual grains of <a href="/wiki/Sediment" title="Sediment">sediment</a>, or the <a href="/wiki/Lithification" title="Lithification">lithified</a> particles in <a href="/wiki/Clastic_rock" title="Clastic rock">clastic rocks</a>.  The term may also be applied to other <a href="/wiki/Granular_material" title="Granular material">granular materials</a>. This is different from the <a href="/wiki/Crystallite" title="Crystallite">crystallite</a> size, which refers to the size of a single <a href="/wiki/Crystal" title="Crystal">crystal</a> inside a particle or grain. A single grain can be composed of several <a href="/wiki/Crystal" title="Crystal">crystals</a>. Granular material can range from very small <a href="/wiki/Colloid" title="Colloid">colloidal particles</a>, through <a href="/wiki/Clay" title="Clay">clay</a>, <a href="/wiki/Silt" title="Silt">silt</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sand" title="Sand">sand</a>, <a href="/wiki/Gravel" title="Gravel">gravel</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Cobble_(geology)" title="Cobble (geology)">cobbles</a>, to <a href="/wiki/Boulder" title="Boulder">boulders</a>.
</p>

<div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:Turmeric_inflorescence.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Turmeric_inflorescence.jpg/250px-Turmeric_inflorescence.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="376" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Turmeric_inflorescence.jpg/500px-Turmeric_inflorescence.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3632" data-file-height="5456"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="capacity building" term="capacity building" wikidataID="Q1417724" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capacity_building" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: capacity building<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capacity_building">Capacity building</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Capacity building</b> (or <b>capacity development, capacity strengthening</b>) is the improvement in an individual's or organization's facility (or capability) "to produce, perform or deploy".<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>&#160;The terms capacity building and capacity development have often been used interchangeably, although a publication by <a href="/wiki/Development_Assistance_Committee" title="Development Assistance Committee">OECD-DAC</a> stated in 2006 that capacity development was the preferable term.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Since the 1950s, international organizations, governments, <a href="/wiki/Non-governmental_organization" title="Non-governmental organization">non-governmental organizations</a> (NGOs) and communities use the concept of capacity building as part of "<a href="/wiki/Socioeconomics" class="mw-redirect" title="Socioeconomics">social and economic development</a>" in national and subnational plans. The <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Development_Programme" title="United Nations Development Programme">United Nations Development Programme</a> defines itself by "capacity development" in the sense of "'how <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Development_Programme" title="United Nations Development Programme">UNDP</a> works" to fulfill its mission.<sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The UN system applies it in almost every sector, including several of the <a href="/wiki/Sustainable_Development_Goals" title="Sustainable Development Goals">Sustainable Development Goals</a> to be achieved by 2030. For example, the <a href="/wiki/Sustainable_Development_Goal_17" title="Sustainable Development Goal 17">Sustainable Development Goal 17</a> advocates for enhanced international support for capacity building in <a href="/wiki/Developing_country" title="Developing country">developing countries</a> to support national plans to implement the <a href="/wiki/Sustainable_Development_Goals" title="Sustainable Development Goals">2030 Agenda</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>&#160; 
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Launching_of_the_%E2%80%9CStrengthening_Capacity_and_Institutional_Reform_for_Green_Growth_and_Sustainable_Development_in_Vietnam%E2%80%9D_Project_(16143587120).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Launching_of_the_%E2%80%9CStrengthening_Capacity_and_Institutional_Reform_for_Green_Growth_and_Sustainable_Development_in_Vietnam%E2%80%9D_Project_%2816143587120%29.jpg/250px-Launching_of_the_%E2%80%9CStrengthening_Capacity_and_Institutional_Reform_for_Green_Growth_and_Sustainable_Development_in_Vietnam%E2%80%9D_Project_%2816143587120%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Launching_of_the_%E2%80%9CStrengthening_Capacity_and_Institutional_Reform_for_Green_Growth_and_Sustainable_Development_in_Vietnam%E2%80%9D_Project_%2816143587120%29.jpg/500px-Launching_of_the_%E2%80%9CStrengthening_Capacity_and_Institutional_Reform_for_Green_Growth_and_Sustainable_Development_in_Vietnam%E2%80%9D_Project_%2816143587120%29.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3173" data-file-height="2122"></a><figcaption>Launching of the "Strengthening Capacity and Institutional Reform for Green Growth and Sustainable Development in Vietnam" Project in 2015</figcaption></figure>

In <a href="/wiki/Systems_engineering" title="Systems engineering">systems engineering</a> and <a href="/wiki/Requirements_engineering" title="Requirements engineering">requirements engineering</a>, a <b>non-functional requirement</b> (<b>NFR</b>) is a <a href="/wiki/Requirement" title="Requirement">requirement</a> that specifies criteria that can be used to judge the operation of a system, rather than specific behaviours. They are contrasted with <a href="/wiki/Functional_requirement" title="Functional requirement">functional requirements</a> that define specific behavior or functions. The plan for implementing <i>functional</i> requirements is detailed in the <a href="/wiki/Systems_design" title="Systems design">system <i>design</i></a>. The plan for implementing <i>non-functional</i> requirements is detailed in the <a href="/wiki/Systems_architecture" title="Systems architecture">system <i>architecture</i></a>, because they are usually <a href="/wiki/Architecturally_significant_requirements" title="Architecturally significant requirements">architecturally significant requirements</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ASR_Chen_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ASR_Chen-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Non-functional requirements are also known as cross-functional requirements by some.<sup id="cite_ref-:1_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

The <b>production of seed</b> is a multibillion-dollar global business, which uses growing facilities and growing locations worldwide. While most of the seed is produced by large specialist growers, large amounts are also produced by small growers who produce only one to a few crop types. The larger companies supply seed both to commercial resellers and wholesalers. The resellers and wholesalers sell to vegetable and fruit growers, and to companies who package seed into packets and sell them on to the amateur gardener.

</div><p></p></div><div name="moisture content" term="moisture content" wikidataID="Q373499" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moisture_content" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: moisture content<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moisture_content">Moisture content</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Water content</b> or <b>moisture content</b> is the quantity of <a href="/wiki/Water" title="Water">water</a> contained in a material, such as <a href="/wiki/Soil" title="Soil">soil</a> (called <i><a href="/wiki/Soil_moisture" title="Soil moisture">soil moisture</a></i>), <a href="/wiki/Rock_(geology)" title="Rock (geology)">rock</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ceramic" title="Ceramic">ceramics</a>, <a href="/wiki/Crops" class="mw-redirect" title="Crops">crops</a>, or <a href="/wiki/Wood" title="Wood">wood</a>. Water content is used in a wide range of scientific and technical areas. It is expressed as a ratio, which can range from 0 (completely dry) to the value of the materials' <a href="/wiki/Porosity" title="Porosity">porosity</a> at saturation. It can be given on a volumetric or gravimetric (mass) basis.

</div><p></p></div><div name="Thespesia lampas" term="Thespesia lampas" wikidataID="Q15357774" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thespesia_lampas" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Thespesia lampas<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thespesia_lampas">Thespesia lampas</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><i><b>Azanza lampas</b></i> is an Asian shrub in the family <a href="/wiki/Malvaceae" title="Malvaceae">Malvaceae</a> and <a href="/wiki/Tribe_(biology)" title="Tribe (biology)">tribe</a> <a href="/wiki/Gossypieae" title="Gossypieae">Gossypieae</a>; its native range is tropical and subtropical Asia.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>  It has yellow flowers, grows up to 3 metres and in Vietnam it is called <i>Tra nh&#7887;</i>.
