<p></p></div><div name="soil samples" term="soil samples" wikidataID="Q877107" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_samples" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: soil samples<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_samples">Soil samples</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">A <b>soil test</b> is a <a href="/wiki/Laboratory" title="Laboratory">laboratory</a> or <a href="/wiki/In_situ" title="In situ">in-situ</a> analysis to determine the chemical, physical or biological characteristics of a soil. Possibly the most widely conducted soil tests are those performed to estimate the plant-available concentrations of <a href="/wiki/Plant_nutrients_in_soil" title="Plant nutrients in soil">nutrients</a> in order to provide <a href="/wiki/Fertilizer" title="Fertilizer">fertilizer</a> recommendations in agriculture. In <a href="/wiki/Geotechnical_engineering" title="Geotechnical engineering">geotechnical engineering</a>, soil tests can be used to determine the current physical state of the soil, the <a href="/wiki/Seepage" title="Seepage">seepage</a> properties, the <a href="/wiki/Shear_strength_(soil)" title="Shear strength (soil)">shear strength</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Deformation_(engineering)" title="Deformation (engineering)">deformation</a> properties of the soil. Other soil tests may be used in <a href="/wiki/Geochemical" class="mw-redirect" title="Geochemical">geochemical</a> or <a href="/wiki/Ecological" class="mw-redirect" title="Ecological">ecological</a> investigations.
</p>
<div title="figure"><figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:20150319-OC-LSC-0534_(16868799182).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/20150319-OC-LSC-0534_%2816868799182%29.jpg/330px-20150319-OC-LSC-0534_%2816868799182%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="300" height="200" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/20150319-OC-LSC-0534_%2816868799182%29.jpg/500px-20150319-OC-LSC-0534_%2816868799182%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/20150319-OC-LSC-0534_%2816868799182%29.jpg/960px-20150319-OC-LSC-0534_%2816868799182%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6000" data-file-height="4004"></a><figcaption>A <a href="/wiki/Horticulture" title="Horticulture">horticulture</a> student taking a soil sample in a garden near <a href="/wiki/Lawrenceville,_Georgia" title="Lawrenceville, Georgia">Lawrenceville, Georgia</a></figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="Technical Textiles" term="Technical Textiles" wikidataID="Q675342" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_textiles" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Technical Textiles<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_textiles">Technical textiles</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Technical textiles</b> are a category of <a href="/wiki/Textile" title="Textile">textiles</a> specifically <a href="/wiki/Textile_manufacturing" title="Textile manufacturing">engineered and manufactured</a> to serve functional purposes beyond traditional apparel and home furnishing applications. These textiles are designed with specific performance characteristics and properties, making them suitable for various industrial, medical, automotive, aerospace, and other technical applications. Unlike conventional textiles used for clothing or decoration, technical textiles are optimized to offer qualities such as strength, durability, <a href="/wiki/Fire-retardant_fabric" title="Fire-retardant fabric">flame resistance</a>, chemical resistance, <a href="/wiki/Moisture_management" title="Moisture management">moisture management</a>, and other specialized functionalities to meet the specific needs of diverse industries and sectors.
</p>

It is a transparent, tasteless, odorless,<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>c<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Color_of_water" title="Color of water">nearly colorless</a> <a href="/wiki/Chemical_substance" class="mw-redirect" title="Chemical substance">chemical substance</a>. It is the main constituent of Earth's <a href="/wiki/Stream" title="Stream">streams</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lake" title="Lake">lakes</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Ocean" title="Ocean">oceans</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Fluid" title="Fluid">fluids</a> of all known living organisms, in which it acts as a <a href="/wiki/Solvent" title="Solvent">solvent</a>. Water, being a <a href="/wiki/Chemical_polarity" title="Chemical polarity">polar</a> molecule, undergoes strong intermolecular <a href="/wiki/Hydrogen_bonding" class="mw-redirect" title="Hydrogen bonding">hydrogen bonding</a> which is a large contributor to its physical and chemical properties.<sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It is vital for all known forms of life, despite not providing <a href="/wiki/Food_energy" title="Food energy">food energy</a> or being an organic <a href="/wiki/Micronutrient" title="Micronutrient">micronutrient</a>. Due to its presence in all organisms, its chemical stability, its worldwide abundance, and its strong polarity relative to its small molecular size, water is often referred to as the "universal solvent".<sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

You can <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_wizard" title="Wikipedia:Article wizard">create a draft and submit it for review</a> or <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_creation/Redirects" title="Wikipedia:Articles for creation/Redirects">request that a redirect be created</a>, but consider checking the search results below to see whether the topic is already covered.</i></p><p></p></div><div name="vegetable oil" term="vegetable oil" wikidataID="Q4739805" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetable_oil" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: vegetable oil<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetable_oil">Vegetable oil</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Vegetable oils</b>, or <b>vegetable fats</b>, are <a href="/wiki/Oil" title="Oil">oils</a> extracted from seeds or from other parts of <a href="/wiki/Edible_plant" class="mw-redirect" title="Edible plant">edible plants</a>. Like <a href="/wiki/Animal_fat" title="Animal fat">animal fats</a>, vegetable fats are <i>mixtures</i> of <a href="/wiki/Triglyceride" title="Triglyceride">triglycerides</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Ullmann_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ullmann-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Soybean_oil" title="Soybean oil">Soybean oil</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rapeseed_oil" title="Rapeseed oil">canola oil</a>, <a href="/wiki/Grape_seed_oil" title="Grape seed oil">grapeseed oil</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Cocoa_butter" title="Cocoa butter">cocoa butter</a> are examples of seed oils, or fats from seeds. <a href="/wiki/Olive_oil" title="Olive oil">Olive oil</a>, <a href="/wiki/Palm_oil" title="Palm oil">palm oil</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Rice_bran_oil" title="Rice bran oil">rice bran oil</a> are examples of fats from other parts of plants. In common usage, vegetable <i>oil</i> may refer exclusively to vegetable fats which are liquid at room temperature.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Vegetable oils are usually edible and are <a href="/wiki/Generally_recognized_as_safe" title="Generally recognized as safe">generally recognized as safe</a> (GRAS) by the <a href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</a> <a href="/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration" title="Food and Drug Administration">Food and Drug Administration</a> (FDA).<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div title="figure"><figure class="mw-halign-center" typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Olive_oil_from_Oneglia.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Olive_oil_from_Oneglia.jpg/250px-Olive_oil_from_Oneglia.jpg" decoding="async" width="145" height="197" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Olive_oil_from_Oneglia.jpg/330px-Olive_oil_from_Oneglia.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1933" data-file-height="2620"></a><figcaption></figcaption></figure></div><p></p></div><div name="biochemistry" term="biochemistry" wikidataID="Q7094" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biochemistry" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: biochemistry<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biochemistry">Biochemistry</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Biochemistry</b>, or <b>biological chemistry</b> (distinct from <a href="/wiki/Chemical_biology" title="Chemical biology">chemical biology</a>), is the study of <a href="/wiki/Chemical_process" title="Chemical process">chemical processes</a> within and relating to living <a href="/wiki/Organism" title="Organism">organisms</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>  A sub-discipline of both <a href="/wiki/Chemistry" title="Chemistry">chemistry</a> and <a href="/wiki/Biology" title="Biology">biology</a>, biochemistry may be divided into three fields: <a href="/wiki/Structural_biology" title="Structural biology">structural biology</a>, <a href="/wiki/Enzymology" class="mw-redirect" title="Enzymology">enzymology</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Metabolism" title="Metabolism">metabolism</a>. Over the last decades of the 20th century, biochemistry has become successful at explaining living processes through these three disciplines.  Almost all <a href="/wiki/List_of_life_sciences" title="List of life sciences">areas of the life sciences</a> are being uncovered and developed through biochemical methodology and research.<sup id="cite_ref-Voet_2005_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Voet_2005-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>  Biochemistry focuses on understanding the chemical basis that allows <a href="/wiki/Biomolecule" title="Biomolecule">biological molecules</a> to give rise to the processes that occur within living <a href="/wiki/Cell_(biology)" title="Cell (biology)">cells</a> and between cells,<sup id="cite_ref-Karp2009_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Karp2009-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> in turn relating greatly to the understanding of <a href="/wiki/Tissue_(biology)" title="Tissue (biology)">tissues</a> and <a href="/wiki/Organ_(anatomy)" class="mw-redirect" title="Organ (anatomy)">organs</a> as well as organism structure and function.<sup id="cite_ref-MillerSpoolman2012_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MillerSpoolman2012-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Biochemistry is closely related to <a href="/wiki/Molecular_biology" title="Molecular biology">molecular biology</a>, the study of the <a href="/wiki/Molecule" title="Molecule">molecular</a> mechanisms of biological phenomena.<sup id="cite_ref-fn_1_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-fn_1-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Gerty_Theresa_Radnitz_Cori_(1896-1957)_and_Carl_Ferdinand_Cori_-_restoration1.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Gerty_Theresa_Radnitz_Cori_%281896-1957%29_and_Carl_Ferdinand_Cori_-_restoration1.jpg/250px-Gerty_Theresa_Radnitz_Cori_%281896-1957%29_and_Carl_Ferdinand_Cori_-_restoration1.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="234" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Gerty_Theresa_Radnitz_Cori_%281896-1957%29_and_Carl_Ferdinand_Cori_-_restoration1.jpg/330px-Gerty_Theresa_Radnitz_Cori_%281896-1957%29_and_Carl_Ferdinand_Cori_-_restoration1.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Gerty_Theresa_Radnitz_Cori_%281896-1957%29_and_Carl_Ferdinand_Cori_-_restoration1.jpg/500px-Gerty_Theresa_Radnitz_Cori_%281896-1957%29_and_Carl_Ferdinand_Cori_-_restoration1.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3098" data-file-height="3822"></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Gerty_Cori" title="Gerty Cori">Gerty Cori</a> and <a href="/wiki/Carl_Cori" class="mw-redirect" title="Carl Cori">Carl Cori</a> jointly won the <a href="/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine" title="Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine">Nobel Prize</a> in 1947 for their discovery of the <a href="/wiki/Cori_cycle" title="Cori cycle">Cori cycle</a> at RPMI.</figcaption></figure>

title="States and union territories of India">state</a> of <a href="/wiki/Maharashtra" title="Maharashtra">Maharashtra</a>. Mumbai is the <a href="/wiki/Financial_centre" title="Financial centre">financial capital</a> and the <a href="/wiki/List_of_cities_in_India_by_population" title="List of cities in India by population">most populous city proper</a> of India, with an estimated population of 12.5 million (1.25&#160;<a href="/wiki/Crore" title="Crore">crore</a>).<sup id="cite_ref-Cities1Lakhandabove_19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Cities1Lakhandabove-19"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Mumbai is the centre of the <a href="/wiki/Mumbai_Metropolitan_Region" title="Mumbai Metropolitan Region">Mumbai Metropolitan Region</a>, which is among the <a href="/wiki/List_of_largest_cities" title="List of largest cities">most populous metropolitan areas in the world</a> with a population of over 23&#160;million (2.3 crore).<sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Mumbai lies on the <a href="/wiki/Konkan" title="Konkan">Konkan</a> coast on the west coast of India and has a deep <a href="/wiki/Natural_harbour" class="mw-redirect" title="Natural harbour">natural harbour</a>. In 2008, Mumbai was named a <a href="/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network#Alpha" title="Globalization and World Cities Research Network">alpha</a> <a href="/wiki/World_city" class="mw-redirect" title="World city">world city</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-lboro2008_21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lboro2008-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Mumbai has the <a href="/wiki/List_of_cities_by_number_of_billionaires" title="List of cities by number of billionaires">highest number of billionaires</a> out of any city in <a href="/wiki/Asia" title="Asia">Asia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>a<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mumbadevi_temple.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Mumbadevi_temple.jpg/250px-Mumbadevi_temple.jpg" decoding="async" width="190" height="285" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Mumbadevi_temple.jpg/330px-Mumbadevi_temple.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Mumbadevi_temple.jpg/500px-Mumbadevi_temple.jpg 2x" data-file-width="533" data-file-height="800"></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Mumba_Devi_Temple" title="Mumba Devi Temple">Mumba Devi Temple</a>, from whom the city of Mumbai may derive its name.</figcaption></figure>

The fiber is almost pure <a href="/wiki/Cellulose" title="Cellulose">cellulose</a> and may contain minor percentages of waxes, fats, pectins, and water. Under natural conditions, cotton bolls facilitate the dispersal of the seeds.

In some countries, <a href="/wiki/Cooking_banana" title="Cooking banana">cooking bananas</a> are called plantains, distinguishing them from <b>dessert bananas</b>. The fruit is variable in size, color and firmness, but is usually elongated and curved, with soft flesh rich in <a href="/wiki/Starch" title="Starch">starch</a> covered with a <a href="/wiki/Peel_(fruit)" title="Peel (fruit)">peel</a>, which may have a variety of colors when ripe. It grows upward in clusters near the top of the plant. Almost all modern edible seedless (<a href="/wiki/Parthenocarpy" title="Parthenocarpy">parthenocarp</a>) cultivated bananas come from two wild species &#8211; <i><a href="/wiki/Musa_acuminata" title="Musa acuminata">Musa acuminata</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Musa_balbisiana" title="Musa balbisiana">Musa balbisiana</a></i>, or their <a href="/wiki/Hybrid_(biology)" title="Hybrid (biology)">hybrids</a>.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Nedravazhakola.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Nedravazhakola.jpg/250px-Nedravazhakola.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Nedravazhakola.jpg/500px-Nedravazhakola.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1536"></a><figcaption><i>Musa</i> 'Nendran' <a href="/wiki/Cultivar" title="Cultivar">cultivar</a>, grown widely in the Indian state of <a href="/wiki/Kerala" title="Kerala">Kerala</a> </figcaption></figure>

class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It reports to both the General Assembly and the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Economic_and_Social_Council" title="United class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> UNCTAD is composed of 195 member states and works with <a href="/wiki/Non-governmental_organization" title="Non-governmental organization">non-governmental organizations</a> worldwide;<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> its permanent secretariat is at <a href="/wiki/UNOG" class="mw-redirect" title="UNOG">UNOG</a> in <a href="/wiki/Geneva" title="Geneva">Geneva</a>, Switzerland.
</p><div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:UNCTAD_Master_Logo_Blue.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/UNCTAD_Master_Logo_Blue.png/250px-UNCTAD_Master_Logo_Blue.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="156" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/UNCTAD_Master_Logo_Blue.png/500px-UNCTAD_Master_Logo_Blue.png 1.5x" data-file-width="900" data-file-height="563"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="closing ceremony" term="closing ceremony" wikidataID="Q3010369" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_ceremony" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: closing ceremony<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_ceremony">Closing ceremony</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">An <b>opening ceremony</b>, <b>grand opening</b>, or <b>ribbon-cutting ceremony</b> marks the official opening of a newly constructed location or the start of an event.<sup id="cite_ref-Adams_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Adams-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Opening ceremonies at significant events such as the <a href="/wiki/Olympic_Games" title="Olympic Games">Olympic Games</a>, <a href="/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup" title="FIFA World Cup">FIFA World Cup</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Rugby_World_Cup" title="Rugby World Cup">Rugby World Cup</a> might involve thousands of participants and be watched worldwide. Such tournaments often also include a <b>closing ceremony</b> at the end of the event.<sup id="cite_ref-time_Ever_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-time_Ever-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

There were no results matching the query.</p><p></p></div><div name="ginning" term="ginning" wikidataID="Q1136790" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginning" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: ginning<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginning">Ginning</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">A <b>cotton gin</b>&#8212;meaning "cotton <a href="/wiki/Engine" title="Engine">engine</a>"<sup id="cite_ref-GeorgiaEncyclopedia_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GeorgiaEncyclopedia-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-merriamwebster_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-merriamwebster-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>&#8212;is a machine that quickly and easily separates <a href="/wiki/Cotton" title="Cotton">cotton</a> fibers from their seeds, enabling much greater productivity than manual cotton separation.<sup id="cite_ref-Roe1916_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Roe1916-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The separated seeds may be used to grow more cotton or to produce <a href="/wiki/Cottonseed_oil" title="Cottonseed oil">cottonseed oil</a>. Handheld roller gins had been used in the <a href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</a> since at earliest 500 and later in other regions.<sup id="cite_ref-LakGin_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LakGin-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Indian <a href="/wiki/Worm_gear" class="mw-redirect" title="Worm gear">worm-gear</a> roller gin was invented sometime around the 16th century<sup id="cite_ref-india_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-india-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> and has, according to Lakwete, remained virtually unchanged up to the present time.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cotton_gin_EWM_2007.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Cotton_gin_EWM_2007.jpg/250px-Cotton_gin_EWM_2007.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Cotton_gin_EWM_2007.jpg/500px-Cotton_gin_EWM_2007.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2820" data-file-height="1856"></a><figcaption>Model of a 19th-century cotton gin on display at the <a href="/wiki/Eli_Whitney_Museum" title="Eli Whitney Museum">Eli Whitney Museum</a> in <a href="/wiki/Hamden,_Connecticut" title="Hamden, Connecticut">Hamden, Connecticut</a></figcaption></figure>  
</div><p></p></div><div name="fatty acids" term="fatty acids" wikidataID="Q61476" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatty_acids" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: fatty acids<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatty_acids">Fatty acids</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">In <a href="/wiki/Chemistry" title="Chemistry">chemistry</a>, particularly in <a href="/wiki/Biochemistry" title="Biochemistry">biochemistry</a>, a <b>fatty acid</b> is a <a href="/wiki/Carboxylic_acid" title="Carboxylic acid">carboxylic acid</a> with an <a href="/wiki/Aliphatic" class="mw-redirect" title="Aliphatic">aliphatic</a> chain, which is either <a href="/wiki/Saturated_and_unsaturated_compounds#Organic_chemistry" title="Saturated and unsaturated compounds">saturated or unsaturated</a>. Most naturally occurring fatty acids have an <a href="/wiki/Branched_chain_fatty_acids" class="mw-redirect" title="Branched chain fatty acids">unbranched chain</a> of an even number of carbon atoms, from 4 to 28.<sup id="cite_ref-iupac_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-iupac-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Fatty acids are a major component of the lipids (up to 70% by weight) in some species such as microalgae<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> but in some other organisms are not found in their standalone form, but instead exist as three main classes of <a href="/wiki/Ester" title="Ester">esters</a>: <a href="/wiki/Triglyceride" title="Triglyceride">triglycerides</a>, <a href="/wiki/Phospholipid" title="Phospholipid">phospholipids</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Cholesteryl_ester" title="Cholesteryl ester">cholesteryl esters</a>. In any of these forms, fatty acids are both important <a href="/wiki/Diet_(nutrition)" title="Diet (nutrition)">dietary</a> sources of fuel for animals and important structural components for <a href="/wiki/Cell_(biology)" title="Cell (biology)">cells</a>.
</p>
<div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Rasyslami.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Rasyslami.jpg/250px-Rasyslami.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/19/Rasyslami.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="432" data-file-height="324"></a><figcaption>Three-dimensional representations of several fatty acids. <a href="/wiki/Saturated_and_unsaturated_compounds" title="Saturated and unsaturated compounds">Saturated</a> fatty acids have perfectly straight chain structure. <a href="/wiki/Unsaturated_compound" class="mw-redirect" title="Unsaturated compound">Unsaturated</a> ones are typically bent, unless they have a <a href="#Unsaturated_fatty_acids">trans</a> configuration.</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="Agricultural Process Engineering" term="Agricultural Process Engineering" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Agricultural%20Process%20Engineering" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Agricultural Process Engineering<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Agricultural%20Process%20Engineering">Agricultural Process Engineering</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">

It is a <a href="/wiki/Field_of_research" class="mw-redirect" title="Field of research">field of research</a> in <a href="/wiki/Computer_science" title="Computer science">computer science</a> that develops and studies methods and <a href="/wiki/Software" title="Software">software</a> that enable machines to perceive their environment and use <a href="/wiki/Machine_learning" title="Machine learning">learning</a> and <a href="/wiki/Intelligence" title="Intelligence">intelligence</a> to take actions that maximize their chances of achieving defined goals.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20211&#8211;4_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20211%E2%80%934-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>

(March 2025)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup> known professionally as <b>Princ od Vranje</b> (<a href="/wiki/Serbian_Cyrillic_alphabet" title="Serbian Cyrillic alphabet">Serbian Cyrillic</a>: <span lang="sr-Cyrl">&#1055;&#1088;&#1080;&#1085;&#1094; &#1086;&#1076; &#1042;&#1088;&#1072;&#1114;&#1077;</span>, <small><a href="/wiki/Literal_translation" title="Literal translation">lit.</a>&#8201;</small><span class="gloss-quot">'</span><span class="gloss-text">Prince of <a href="/wiki/Vranje" title="Vranje">Vranje</a></span><span class="gloss-quot">'</span>) or simply <b>Princ</b>, is a Serbian singer. He represented <a href="/wiki/Serbia_in_the_Eurovision_Song_Contest_2025" title="Serbia in the Eurovision Song Contest 2025">Serbia</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest_2025" title="Eurovision Song Contest 2025">Eurovision Song Contest 2025</a> with the song "<a href="/wiki/Mila_(song)" title="Mila (song)">Mila</a>".
</p>
<div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:PrepartyES_-_Princ_02.jpg" class="mw-file-description" title="Zdravkovi&#263; in 2025"><img alt="Zdravkovi&#263; in 2025" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/PrepartyES_-_Princ_02.jpg/250px-PrepartyES_-_Princ_02.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="375" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/PrepartyES_-_Princ_02.jpg/500px-PrepartyES_-_Princ_02.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="3743" data-file-height="5615"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="Peltier module" term="Peltier module" wikidataID="Q135350207" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peltier_module" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Peltier module<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peltier_module">Peltier module</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Thermoelectric heat pumps</b> use the <a href="/wiki/Thermoelectric_effect" title="Thermoelectric effect">thermoelectric effect</a>, specifically the <a href="/wiki/Peltier_effect" class="mw-redirect" title="Peltier effect">Peltier effect</a>, to heat or cool materials by applying an <a href="/wiki/Electrical_current" class="mw-redirect" title="Electrical current">electrical current</a> across them. A Peltier cooler, heater, or <a href="/wiki/Thermoelectric" class="mw-redirect" title="Thermoelectric">thermoelectric</a> heat pump is a <a href="/wiki/Solid-state_physics" title="Solid-state physics">solid-state</a> active <a href="/wiki/Heat_pump" title="Heat pump">heat pump</a> which transfers heat from one side of the device to the other, with consumption of <a href="/wiki/Electrical_energy" title="Electrical energy">electrical energy</a>, depending on the direction of the current. Such an instrument is also called a <b>Peltier device</b>, <b>Peltier heat pump</b>, <b>solid state refrigerator</b>, or <b>thermoelectric cooler</b> (<b>TEC</b>) and occasionally a <b>thermoelectric battery</b>. It can be used either for heating or for cooling,<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> although in practice the main application is cooling since heating can be achieved with simpler devices (with <a href="/wiki/Joule_heating" title="Joule heating">Joule heating</a>).
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Peltierelement.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Peltierelement.png/330px-Peltierelement.png" decoding="async" width="310" height="171" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Peltierelement.png/500px-Peltierelement.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Peltierelement.png/960px-Peltierelement.png 2x" data-file-width="2700" data-file-height="1485"></a><figcaption>Peltier element schematic. Thermoelectric legs are thermally in parallel and electrically in series.</figcaption></figure>
</div><p></p></div><div name="micronaire" term="micronaire" wikidataID="Q904443" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micronaire" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: micronaire<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micronaire">Micronaire</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><a href="/wiki/Textile" title="Textile">Textile</a> <a href="/wiki/Fiber" title="Fiber">fibers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Thread_(yarn)" title="Thread (yarn)">threads</a>, <a href="/wiki/Yarn" title="Yarn">yarns</a> and <a href="/wiki/Fabric" class="mw-redirect" title="Fabric">fabrics</a> are measured in a multiplicity of units. 
</p>
<div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Thread2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ad/Thread2.jpg" decoding="async" width="212" height="491" class="mw-file-element" data-file-width="212" data-file-height="491"></a><figcaption>Thread made from two threads plied together, each consisting of three yarns</figcaption></figure></div><p></p></div><div name="Paras" term="Paras" wikidataID="Q404205" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paras" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Paras<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paras">Paras</a></p><p></p></div><div name="nanotechnology" term="nanotechnology" wikidataID="Q11468" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanotechnology" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: nanotechnology<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanotechnology">Nanotechnology</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Nanotechnology</b> is the manipulation of matter with at least one dimension sized from 1 to 100 <a href="/wiki/Nanometers" class="mw-redirect" title="Nanometers">nanometers</a> (nm). At this scale, commonly known as the <b>nanoscale</b>, <a href="/wiki/Surface_area" title="Surface area">surface area</a> and <a href="/wiki/Quantum_mechanical" class="mw-redirect" title="Quantum mechanical">quantum mechanical</a> effects become important in describing properties of matter. This definition of nanotechnology includes all types of research and technologies that deal with these special properties. It is common to see the plural form "nanotechnologies" as well as "nanoscale technologies" to refer to research and applications whose common trait is scale.<sup id="cite_ref-Engines1_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Engines1-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> An earlier understanding of nanotechnology referred to the particular technological goal of precisely manipulating atoms and molecules for fabricating macroscale products, now referred to as <a href="/wiki/Molecular_nanotechnology" title="Molecular nanotechnology">molecular nanotechnology</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Nanotsystems_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Nanotsystems-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Fullerene_Nanogears_-_GPN-2000-001535.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Fullerene_Nanogears_-_GPN-2000-001535.jpg/330px-Fullerene_Nanogears_-_GPN-2000-001535.jpg" decoding="async" width="300" height="198" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Fullerene_Nanogears_-_GPN-2000-001535.jpg/500px-Fullerene_Nanogears_-_GPN-2000-001535.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Fullerene_Nanogears_-_GPN-2000-001535.jpg/960px-Fullerene_Nanogears_-_GPN-2000-001535.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2808" data-file-height="1851"></a><figcaption>Fullerene nanogears</figcaption></figure>

<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/&#609;/: 'g' in 'guy'">&#609;</span><span title="'l' in 'lie'">l</span><span title="/a&#618;/: 'i' in 'tide'">a&#618;</span><span title="/&#712;/: primary stress follows">&#712;</span><span title="'s' in 'sigh'">s</span><span title="/i&#720;/: 'ee' in 'fleece'">i&#720;</span><span title="'m' in 'my'">m</span><span title="/&#618;/: 'i' in 'kit'">&#618;</span><span title="'k' in 'kind'">k</span></span>/</a></span></span><sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>) is a number from 0 to 100 assigned to a food, with pure glucose arbitrarily given the value of 100, which represents the relative rise in the blood glucose level two hours after consuming that food.<sup id="cite_ref-glycemic1_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-glycemic1-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The GI of a specific food depends primarily on the type of <a href="/wiki/Carbohydrate" title="Carbohydrate">carbohydrate</a> it contains, but is also affected by the amount of entrapment of the carbohydrate molecules within the food, the fat, protein content of the food, the moisture and fiber content, the amount of organic acids (or their salts) (e.g., citric or acetic acid), and the method of cooking.  GI tables, which list many types of foods and their GIs, are available.<sup id="cite_ref-glycemicedge_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-glycemicedge-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A food is considered to have a  <i>low GI</i> if it is 55 or less; <i>high GI</i> if 70 or more; and <i>mid-range GI</i> if 56 to 69.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Suckale08_fig3_glucose_insulin_day.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Suckale08_fig3_glucose_insulin_day.png/250px-Suckale08_fig3_glucose_insulin_day.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Suckale08_fig3_glucose_insulin_day.png/500px-Suckale08_fig3_glucose_insulin_day.png 1.5x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="600"></a><figcaption>Graph depicting blood sugar change during a day with three meals.</figcaption></figure>

</p>
<div title="figure"><a href="/wiki/File:ICARDA_logo.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/af/ICARDA_logo.png/250px-ICARDA_logo.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="80" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/a/af/ICARDA_logo.png 1.5x" data-file-width="400" data-file-height="128"></a></div><p></p></div><div name="Microorganisms" term="Microorganisms" wikidataID="Q39833" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microorganisms" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Microorganisms<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microorganisms">Microorganisms</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">A <b>microorganism</b>, or <b>microbe</b>,<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>a<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> is an <a href="/wiki/Organism" title="Organism">organism</a> of <a href="/wiki/Microscopic_scale" title="Microscopic scale">microscopic</a> size, which may exist in its <a href="/wiki/Unicellular_organism" title="Unicellular organism">single-celled</a> form or as a <a href="/wiki/Colony_(biology)#Microbial_colonies" title="Colony (biology)">colony of cells</a>. The possible existence of unseen microbial life was suspected from antiquity, with an early attestation in <a href="/wiki/Jain_literature" title="Jain literature">Jain literature</a> authored in 6th-century&#160;BC India. The scientific study of microorganisms began with their observation under the <a href="/wiki/Microscope" title="Microscope">microscope</a> in the 1670s by <a href="/wiki/Anton_van_Leeuwenhoek" class="mw-redirect" title="Anton van Leeuwenhoek">Anton van Leeuwenhoek</a>. In the 1850s, <a href="/wiki/Louis_Pasteur" title="Louis Pasteur">Louis Pasteur</a> found that microorganisms caused <a href="/wiki/Food_spoilage" title="Food spoilage">food spoilage</a>, debunking the theory of <a href="/wiki/Spontaneous_generation" title="Spontaneous generation">spontaneous generation</a>. In the 1880s, <a href="/wiki/Robert_Koch" title="Robert Koch">Robert Koch</a> discovered that microorganisms caused the diseases <a href="/wiki/Tuberculosis" title="Tuberculosis">tuberculosis</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cholera" title="Cholera">cholera</a>, <a href="/wiki/Diphtheria" title="Diphtheria">diphtheria</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Anthrax" title="Anthrax">anthrax</a>.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:E_coli_at_10000x,_original.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/E_coli_at_10000x%2C_original.jpg/500px-E_coli_at_10000x%2C_original.jpg" decoding="async" width="340" height="247" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/E_coli_at_10000x%2C_original.jpg/960px-E_coli_at_10000x%2C_original.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="2598" data-file-height="1889"></a><figcaption>A <a href="/wiki/Colony_(biology)#Microbial_colonies" title="Colony (biology)">cluster</a> of <i><a href="/wiki/Escherichia_coli" title="Escherichia coli">Escherichia coli</a></i> bacteria magnified 10,000 times</figcaption></figure>

It is a <a href="/wiki/Metal" title="Metal">metal</a> that belongs to the <a href="/wiki/First_transition_series" class="mw-redirect" title="First transition series">first transition series</a> and <a href="/wiki/Group_8_element" title="Group 8 element">group 8</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Periodic_table" title="Periodic table">periodic table</a>. It is, by mass, the <a href="/wiki/Abundance_of_the_chemical_elements#Earth" title="Abundance of the chemical elements">most common element</a> on <a href="/wiki/Earth" title="Earth">Earth</a>, forming much of Earth's <a href="/wiki/Outer_core" class="mw-redirect" title="Outer core">outer</a> and <a href="/wiki/Inner_core" class="mw-redirect" title="Inner core">inner core</a>. It is the fourth most <a href="/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth%27s_crust" title="Abundance of elements in Earth's crust">abundant element</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Earth%27s_crust" title="Earth's crust">Earth's crust</a>. In its metallic state it was mainly <a href="/wiki/Meteoric_iron" title="Meteoric iron">deposited by</a> <a href="/wiki/Meteorite" title="Meteorite">meteorites</a>.

One form of tribunal is a <a href="/wiki/Court" title="Court">court</a>. The tribunal, which may occur before a <a href="/wiki/Judge" title="Judge">judge</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jury" title="Jury">jury</a>, or other designated <a href="/wiki/Trier_of_fact" title="Trier of fact">trier of fact</a>, aims to achieve a resolution to their dispute.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Le_Lit_de_justice_de_Vend%C3%B4me.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Le_Lit_de_justice_de_Vend%C3%B4me.jpg/250px-Le_Lit_de_justice_de_Vend%C3%B4me.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="304" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Le_Lit_de_justice_de_Vend%C3%B4me.jpg/500px-Le_Lit_de_justice_de_Vend%C3%B4me.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="1475" data-file-height="1794"></a><figcaption>Trial of <a href="/wiki/Jean_II,_Duke_of_Alen%C3%A7on" title="Jean II, Duke of Alen&#231;on">Jean II, Duke of Alen&#231;on</a>, October 1458</figcaption></figure></div><p></p></div><div name="Leaf rust resistance" term="Leaf rust resistance" wikidataID="Q100683084" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf_rust_resistance" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Leaf rust resistance<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf_rust_resistance">Leaf rust resistance</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Wheat leaf rust</b> (<i><b>Puccinia triticina</b></i>) is a fungal disease that affects <a href="/wiki/Wheat" title="Wheat">wheat</a>, <a href="/wiki/Barley" title="Barley">barley</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rye" title="Rye">rye</a> stems, leaves and grains. In <a href="/wiki/Temperate_zones" class="mw-redirect" title="Temperate zones">temperate zones</a> it is destructive on <a href="/wiki/Winter_wheat" title="Winter wheat">winter wheat</a> because the pathogen <a href="/wiki/Overwinter" class="mw-redirect" title="Overwinter">overwinters</a>. Infections can lead up to 20% <a href="/wiki/Crop_yield" title="Crop yield">yield</a> loss. The pathogen is a <i><a href="/wiki/Puccinia" title="Puccinia">Puccinia</a></i> <a href="/wiki/Rust_(fungus)" title="Rust (fungus)">rust fungus</a>. It is the most prevalent of all the wheat rust diseases, occurring in most wheat-growing regions.<sup id="cite_ref-Liu-et-al-2013_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Liu-et-al-2013-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> It causes serious <a href="/wiki/Epidemic" title="Epidemic">epidemics</a> in <a href="/wiki/North_America" title="North America">North America</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mexico" title="Mexico">Mexico</a> and <a href="/wiki/South_America" title="South America">South America</a> and is a devastating seasonal disease in <a href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</a>. <i>P. triticina</i> is <a href="/wiki/Heteroecious" title="Heteroecious">heteroecious</a>, requiring two distinct hosts (alternate hosts).<sup id="cite_ref-Liu-et-al-2013_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Liu-et-al-2013-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Bolton-et-al-2008_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bolton-et-al-2008-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>

It is bordered by the <a href="/wiki/Arabian_Sea" title="Arabian Sea">Arabian Sea</a> to the west, the Indian states of <a href="/wiki/Karnataka" title="Karnataka">Karnataka</a> and <a href="/wiki/Goa" title="Goa">Goa</a> to the south, <a href="/wiki/Telangana" title="Telangana">Telangana</a> to the southeast and <a href="/wiki/Chhattisgarh" title="Chhattisgarh">Chhattisgarh</a> to the east, <a href="/wiki/Gujarat" title="Gujarat">Gujarat</a> and <a href="/wiki/Madhya_Pradesh" title="Madhya Pradesh">Madhya Pradesh</a> to the north, and the Indian <a href="/wiki/Union_territory" title="Union territory">union territory</a> of <a href="/wiki/Dadra_and_Nagar_Haveli_and_Daman_and_Diu" title="Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu">Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu</a> to the northwest.<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Maharashtra is the <a href="/wiki/List_of_states_and_union_territories_of_India_by_population" title="List of states and union territories of India by population">second-most populous state</a> in India, the third-most populous country subdivision in <a href="/wiki/South_Asia" title="South Asia">South Asia</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/List_of_first-level_administrative_divisions_by_population" title="List of first-level administrative divisions by population">fourth-most populous</a> in the world.

<p></p></div><div name="Atomic Force Microscopy" term="Atomic Force Microscopy" wikidataID="Q10329629" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_Force_Microscopy" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Atomic Force Microscopy<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_Force_Microscopy">Atomic Force Microscopy</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Atomic force microscopy</b> (<b>AFM</b>) or <b>scanning force microscopy</b> (<b>SFM</b>) is a very-high-resolution type of <a href="/wiki/Scanning_probe_microscopy" title="Scanning probe microscopy">scanning probe microscopy</a> (SPM), with demonstrated resolution on the order of fractions of a nanometer, more than 1000 times better than the <a href="/wiki/Diffraction-limited_system" title="Diffraction-limited system">optical diffraction limit</a>.
</p>
<div title="figure"><figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Atomic_force_microscope_block_diagram.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Atomic_force_microscope_block_diagram.svg/250px-Atomic_force_microscope_block_diagram.svg.png" decoding="async" width="240" height="223" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Atomic_force_microscope_block_diagram.svg/500px-Atomic_force_microscope_block_diagram.svg.png 1.5x" data-file-width="926" data-file-height="859"></a><figcaption>An AFM generates images by scanning a small cantilever over the surface of a sample. The sharp tip on the end of the cantilever contacts the surface, bending the cantilever and changing the amount of laser light reflected into the photodiode. </div><p></p></div><div name="Anuj Kumar" term="Anuj Kumar" wikidataID="Q17386210" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anuj_Kumar" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: Anuj Kumar<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anuj_Kumar">Anuj Kumar</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para"><b>Anuj Kumar Chaudhary</b> (born 5 August) is a retired Indian freestyle wrestler and  Additional Superintendent of Police (ASP) in <a href="/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh" title="Uttar Pradesh">Uttar Pradesh</a>. Modern manufactured sewing threads may be finished with <a href="/wiki/Wax" title="Wax">wax</a> or other <a href="/wiki/Lubricant" title="Lubricant">lubricants</a> to withstand the stresses involved in sewing.<sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Embroidery_thread" title="Embroidery thread">Embroidery threads</a> are yarns specifically designed for <a href="/wiki/Needlework" title="Needlework">needlework</a>. Yarn can be made of a number of natural or synthetic materials, and comes in a variety of colors and thicknesses (referred to as "weights"). Although yarn may be <a href="/wiki/Dyeing" title="Dyeing">dyed</a> different colours, most yarns are solid coloured with a uniform <a href="/wiki/Hue" title="Hue">hue</a>.

You can <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_wizard" title="Wikipedia:Article wizard">create a draft and submit it for review</a> or <a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_creation/Redirects" title="Wikipedia:Articles for creation/Redirects">request that a redirect be created</a>, but consider checking the search results below to see whether the topic is already covered.</i></p><p></p></div><div name="gene" term="gene" wikidataID="Q7187" wikipedia_url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene" role="ami_entry"><p>search term: gene<br><span>Wikipedia URL: </span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene">Gene</a></p><p class="wpage_first_para">In <a href="/wiki/Biology" title="Biology">biology</a>, the word <b>gene</b> has two meanings. The Mendelian gene is a basic unit of <a href="/wiki/Heredity" title="Heredity">heredity</a>. The molecular gene is a sequence of <a href="/wiki/Nucleotide" title="Nucleotide">nucleotides</a> in <a href="/wiki/DNA" title="DNA">DNA</a> that is transcribed to produce <a href="/wiki/RNA" title="RNA">RNA</a>. There are two types of molecular genes: protein-coding genes and non-coding genes.<sup id="cite_ref-mendgene2_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mendgene2-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-MedlinePlus_2020_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MedlinePlus_2020-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During <a href="/wiki/Gene_expression" title="Gene expression">gene expression</a> (the synthesis of <a href="/wiki/Gene_product" title="Gene product">RNA or protein</a> from a gene), DNA is first <a href="/wiki/Transcription_(biology)" title="Transcription (biology)">copied into RNA</a>. RNA can be <a href="/wiki/Non-coding_RNA" title="Non-coding RNA">directly functional</a> or be the intermediate <a href="/wiki/Protein_biosynthesis" title="Protein biosynthesis">template</a> for the synthesis of a protein.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Gregor_Mendel_-_American_Breeders_Magazine,_1910.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Photograph of Gregor Mendel" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Gregor_Mendel_-_American_Breeders_Magazine%2C_1910.jpg/250px-Gregor_Mendel_-_American_Breeders_Magazine%2C_1910.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="256" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Gregor_Mendel_-_American_Breeders_Magazine%2C_1910.jpg/330px-Gregor_Mendel_-_American_Breeders_Magazine%2C_1910.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Gregor_Mendel_-_American_Breeders_Magazine%2C_1910.jpg/500px-Gregor_Mendel_-_American_Breeders_Magazine%2C_1910.jpg 2x" data-file-width="780" data-file-height="1000"></a><figcaption>Gregor Mendel</figcaption></figure>

The technology provides end users a variety of aesthetic free-form building designs. Custom-made structures are <a href="/wiki/Engineering" title="Engineering">engineered</a> and fabricated to meet worldwide structural, <a href="/wiki/Flame_retardant" title="Flame retardant">flame retardant</a>, weather-resistant, and natural force requirements.
Fabric structures are considered a sub-category of <a href="/wiki/Tensile_structure" title="Tensile structure">tensile structure</a>.

Biological molecules such as <a href="/wiki/RNA" title="RNA">RNA</a> and <a href="/wiki/DNA" title="DNA">DNA</a> are considered by some as data storage.<sup id="cite_ref-rna_1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rna-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Recording may be accomplished with virtually any form of <a href="/wiki/Energy" title="Energy">energy</a>. Electronic data storage requires electrical power to store and retrieve data.

The <a href="/wiki/Phonograph_cylinder" title="Phonograph cylinder">phonograph cylinder</a> is a storage medium. The phonograph may be considered a storage device, especially as machines of this vintage were able to record on blank cylinders.</figcaption></figure>

Proteins perform a vast array of functions within organisms, including <a href="/wiki/Enzyme_catalysis" title="Enzyme catalysis">catalysing metabolic reactions</a>, <a href="/wiki/DNA_replication" title="DNA replication">DNA replication</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cell_signaling" title="Cell signaling">responding to stimuli</a>, providing <a href="/wiki/Cytoskeleton" title="Cytoskeleton">structure to cells</a> and <a href="/wiki/Fibrous_protein" title="Fibrous protein">organisms</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Intracellular_transport" title="Intracellular transport">transporting molecules</a> from one location to another. Proteins differ from one another primarily in their sequence of amino acids, which is dictated by the <a href="/wiki/Nucleic_acid_sequence" title="Nucleic acid sequence">nucleotide sequence</a> of their <a href="/wiki/Gene" title="Gene">genes</a>, and which usually results in <a href="/wiki/Protein_folding" title="Protein folding">protein folding</a> into a specific <a href="/wiki/Protein_structure" title="Protein structure">3D structure</a> that determines its activity.
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Myoglobin.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Myoglobin.png/250px-Myoglobin.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="253" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Myoglobin.png/500px-Myoglobin.png 1.5x" data-file-width="1159" data-file-height="1173"></a><figcaption>A representation of the 3D structure of the protein <a href="/wiki/Myoglobin" title="Myoglobin">myoglobin</a> showing turquoise <a href="/wiki/Alpha_helix" title="Alpha helix">&#945;-helices</a>. This protein was the first to have its structure solved by <a href="/wiki/X-ray_crystallography" title="X-ray crystallography">X-ray crystallography</a>. Toward the right-center among the coils, a <a href="/wiki/Prosthetic_group" title="Prosthetic group">prosthetic group</a> called a <a href="/wiki/Heme_group" class="mw-redirect" title="Heme group">heme group</a> (shown in gray) with a bound oxygen molecule (red).</figcaption></figure>

class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>) is any <a href="/wiki/Chord_(music)" title="Chord (music)">chord</a> with predominant (subdominant) <a href="/wiki/Function_(music)" title="Function (music)">function</a>, normally <a href="/wiki/Resolution_(music)" title="Resolution (music)">resolving to</a> a <a href="/wiki/Dominant_(music)" title="Dominant (music)">dominant</a> chord.<sup id="cite_ref-B&amp;S_3-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-B&amp;S-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Examples of predominant chords are the <a href="/wiki/Subdominant" title="Subdominant">subdominant</a> (IV, iv), <a href="/wiki/Supertonic" title="Supertonic">supertonic</a> (ii, ii&#176;), <a href="/wiki/Neapolitan_sixth" class="mw-redirect" title="Neapolitan sixth">Neapolitan sixth</a> and <a href="/wiki/Augmented_sixth_chord" title="Augmented sixth chord">German sixth</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-B&amp;S_3-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-B&amp;S-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Other examples are the <a href="/wiki/Secondary_dominant" class="mw-redirect" title="Secondary dominant">secondary dominant</a> (V/V) and <a href="/wiki/Secondary_leading_tone_chord" class="mw-redirect" title="Secondary leading tone chord">secondary leading tone chord</a>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="uncited examples after cited examples. (January 2017)">citation needed</span></a></i>]</sup> Predominant chords may lead to secondary dominants.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Predominant chords both expand away from the <a href="/wiki/Tonic_(music)" title="Tonic (music)">tonic</a> <i>and</i> lead to the dominant, affirming the dominant's pull to the tonic.<sup id="cite_ref-Aural_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Aural-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Thus they lack the stability of the tonic and the drive towards resolution of the dominant.<sup id="cite_ref-Aural_5-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Aural-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The predominant <a href="/wiki/Diatonic_function" class="mw-redirect" title="Diatonic function">harmonic function</a> is part of the fundamental <a href="/wiki/Chord_progression" title="Chord progression">harmonic progression</a> of many classical works.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Submediant" title="Submediant">submediant</a> (vi) may be considered a predominant chord or a tonic substitute.<sup id="cite_ref-Analyzing_7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Analyzing-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><div title="figure"><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.png/250px-V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="127" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.png/500px-V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.png 1.5x" data-file-width="1008" data-file-height="514"></a><figcaption>V of V in C, four-part harmony <span class="ext-phonos"><span data-nosnippet="" id="ooui-php-1" class="noexcerpt ext-phonos-PhonosButton oo-ui-widget oo-ui-widget-enabled oo-ui-buttonElement oo-ui-buttonElement-frameless oo-ui-iconElement oo-ui-labelElement oo-ui-buttonWidget" data-ooui='{"_":"mw.Phonos.PhonosButton","href":"\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/transcoded\/c\/c0\/V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.mid\/V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.mid.mp3","rel":["nofollow"],"framed":false,"icon":"volumeUp","label":{"html":"Play"},"data":{"ipa":"","text":"","lang":"en","wikibase":"","file":"V of V in C four-part harmony.mid"},"classes":["noexcerpt","ext-phonos-PhonosButton"]}'><a role="button" tabindex="0" href="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/c/c0/V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.mid/V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.mid.mp3" rel="nofollow" aria-label="Play audio" title="Play audio" class="oo-ui-buttonElement-button"><span class="oo-ui-iconElement-icon oo-ui-icon-volumeUp"></span><span class="oo-ui-labelElement-label">Play</span><span class="oo-ui-indicatorElement-indicator oo-ui-indicatorElement-noIndicator"></span></a></span><sup class="ext-phonos-attribution noexcerpt navigation-not-searchable"><a href="/wiki/File:V_of_V_in_C_four-part_harmony.mid" title="File:V of V in C four-part harmony.mid">&#9432;</a></sup></span>.</figcaption></figure>
